articles.title: Ego Death on 9/11
articles.summary: Heartbroken and opened in the aftermath of a national tragedy, a former marketing professional embarks on a life in the dharma. The post Ego Death on 9/11 appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
articles.content:
September 2001. I’m a third-generation advertising guy, nearing 40, recently married, going bald, and just fit enough to get by. By day I work as an art director at a big-name agency; by morning, I meditate—rhythm of breath steadying me amid Manhattan’s roar. Six years sober in a Twelve Step community, where the faces are as familiar as family. Just another Tuesday: coffee on my breath, subway air thick with pastry and steel.

On my way to work, I overhear strange conversations in the subway car concerning extraordinary events happening on the streets above. Whispers turn urgent, phones appear in hands. As the train arrives at Union Square, I exit to find commotion at street level—faces tilted skyward, traffic frozen. Walking to University Place, I look downtown expecting to see the familiar Twin Towers standing sentinel against the blue September sky.

In that instant, my life begins to unravel. The towers are obscured by tremendous plumes of black smoke that billow against the cloudless sky. As a kid, my dad brought me downtown to watch the towers as they were constructed; they were bland, characterless boxes, yet as integral to Manhattan’s skyline as the Empire State and Chrysler buildings. I become aware of the people around me, frozen in tableaux of horror, some covering their mouths with trembling hands, others holding phones to their ears, shouting or whispering, I can’t tell. Sirens wail from every direction, their urgent screams slicing through the stunned silence.

Crowds have gathered on sidewalks and streets, bodies pressed together in wordless communion, peering up at a large outdoor advertising screen, showing repeating videos of the towers’ collapse. Gasps, screams, a shivering realization that if the occupants weren’t all evacuated, they were swallowed, crushed, entombed in a concrete grave. I don’t yet know that several firemen I’ve met at Alcoholics Anonymous are already gone, their laughter silenced beneath tons of steel and glass. I’m in a daze, or what I will later learn to be a dissociative state. Nothing feels real—the world suddenly rendered in watercolor rather than sharp focus. I no longer see objects moving in continuity but in discontinuous, scattered frames. Sounds are muted, cotton-wrapped; I can’t feel the ground beneath me, it seems like a lucid dream, for I am just as powerless to speak as in those nightmares where your voice evaporates when you need it most.

The subways are closed, all the bridges as well, the sole exception being the 59th Street Bridge, the only way back home to Brooklyn. It’s a long walk ahead of me, but there’s nowhere else to go but forward, with no clear sense of what “forward” means in a world suddenly turned inside out. I walk in a loose group of work colleagues, our usual banter about deadlines and clients now painfully irrelevant. There’s little, if any, conversation going on. When someone does speak, it’s barely above a whisper—as if raising our voices might break whatever fragile thread is holding us together in this new, terrifying reality.

I spend the months afterward still walking about in a trance, fully experiencing a crisis that peels back layers of myself I never knew existed. While New York’s bars fill with those numbing themselves to pain, glasses clinking in desperate toasts to lost normalcy, as a recovering alcoholic that option is not available to me. So I fall into what one psychiatrist diagnoses as a “post-traumatic episode” without any substance to ease the shock—raw nerves exposed to every painful stimulus.

And then comes the return of long-repressed memories from a childhood spent in a violent household, reactivated by my current state of helplessness, powerlessness, outright fear. They rise like ghosts from a disturbed grave.

Feelings of low self-esteem, suppressed during years of addiction and living on society’s margins, rush up from my abdomen in spasms that double me over when I’m alone. “You’re worthless, you’re a momma’s boy, you’re a waste.” My father’s home-from-the-bars drunken rants return as an unrelenting voice in my head, each syllable a hammer blow. I can hear the screams from my parents’ bedroom as if they’re happening right now, not thirty years past—the sound of breaking glass, of flesh striking flesh, of childhood terror.

My wife finds me shaking on the couch in a fetal position. I’m sweating through my T-shirt, gulping for air like a landed fish, in the grip of a panic attack, my stomach cement-hard yet churning with acid. In my mind, movie screens play horror films—images of being alone in the world, unloved, adrift in cosmic indifference. My life no longer makes sense. September 11 has pulled away the delusion of certainty, of safety, revealing a world where nothing is guaranteed, where everything can vanish in smoke as quickly as those towers fell. And what the hell am I doing with my life? Working in advertising—crafting lies about happiness in bottles and boxes!

The following months of 2001 alternate between numbness and self-hatred sharp enough to cut. There is so much healing needed, an ocean of pain to cross without drowning. My self-care consists of weekly visits to Buddhist centers where incense sweetens the air, daily Twelve Step meetings in church basements where coffee burns bitter in Styrofoam cups, and morning meditations on a cushion that never feels quite comfortable. Perhaps this routine would suffice for most people, but not for me—the foundations have been too thoroughly shaken.

On days I make it to work, I head straight to my office, closing the door behind me to separate myself from the busy, fluorescent-lit, red-carpeted hallways where life continues as if the world hasn’t fundamentally changed. I sit dazed before an improbably large desktop computer, lost in the virtual chambers of the early internet where banner ads flash with false promises. My life, which only a few weeks ago seemed to make sense, providing some form of coherence, has revealed itself to be empty, inconsequential, futile, thoroughly pointless. “Meet the new Toyorati Renaissance. A sleek, beautiful exterior with luxurious padded seating, and don’t forget that powerful 300-horsepower engine!” “Are you anxious? Depressed? Burnt out? Feeling like an imposter, or annoyed by everything? Emo-Numb™ is there for you.” This is what my life has become? Crafting slogans while the world burns?

This is what my life has become? Crafting slogans while the world burns?

Morning meditations are grinds, but I turn to them in the hope of finding the slightest foothold on sanity, a toehold on the cliff face of despair. Instead of observing thoughts like clouds passing through the sky as I’ve been taught, I resist them obsessively, trying to push them away with the force of will. Rather than listening to entombed fears, I crave numbness like an old addiction. I’m falling into the trap of using meditation as avoidance, a spiritual bypass, instead of greeting the dread, the inner shaming voices from which I’ve been running since childhood.

I experience, firsthand, a state of mind where no thought, emotion, or feeling can be put aside, distracted, alleviated; flooding images of a childhood spent lonely, yearning for friends, terrified of social groups—all my practice can offer is a way to hold these human experiences, each comprised of energies that must express themselves. Practice doesn’t allow me to gain distance from anything, but at least I’m learning how to “be with it, no matter how painful it is”—to sit in the fire without being consumed.

Desperation finally motivates me to seek out more support. I find a Buddhist therapist whose office smells of sandalwood, whose sessions create a safe space for sharing thoughts and feelings that feel too shameful to voice elsewhere. Session after session, I practice locating fears as they arise not only in my mind but in my stomach, chest, and shoulders—the geography of anxiety mapped on my body. I contact the long-buried feelings of a terrified 6-year-old shaking in bed as his drunk father arrives home, keys jangling like warning bells; I learn to console this child and provide him with a new sense of security that no one offered then. I rekindle studies in the Buddha’s teachings and seek retreats with monks who embody the kindness and balance I desperately need—their presence itself a teaching in stillness.

During this period, I find a Buddhist community, populated by others who, like me, grew up in punk circles and wound up covered with tattoos, and are recovering from substance dependencies, trying to make sense of the world; finally, I’m in a place where I feel I belong—where my history isn’t something to hide but part of the path that brought me here.

I’ve spent more days than I can count in the marketing profession, watching the city pulse below through plate glass windows as I craft campaigns for products nobody needs, the sky changing colors while I stay fixed to my ergonomic chair. Fifteen years of my life dedicated to convincing others that happiness is a matter of purchasing useless software apps and needless tech, that fulfillment comes boxed and shrink-wrapped. My business card states “associate creative director” and even “brand strategist,” impressive titles that suggest I possess skills of some value beyond making people want things they don’t need. The pay is fine—it always has been. I have enough to pay the mortgage on an apartment too small for its price and travel to places I photograph more than experience.

But then the world breaks open, spilling its messy truth. Suffering floods the same screens where I once pitched campaigns for soda and SUVs. Something shifts—quietly at first, then with the force of an earthquake. I feel it in my bones: a tectonic realignment of values. The old narrative begins to collapse. “Does any of this matter?” The question nags at me through meetings and missed deadlines. The Buddha once left behind a palace. I’m just trying to leave behind a brand deck. Yet the act feels no less radical. Even “quiet quitting” feels like a rebellion against the lie I helped sell. Every step away from that world is a step toward remembering what I truly am beneath the costume.

Walking away isn’t easy—fear clutches at my ankles with every step. Financial security has been my religion for so long that abandoning it feels like stepping off a cliff without knowing how far I’ll fall or what waits at the bottom. Yet something pulls me forward, a current stronger than fear. I remember how the Buddha himself left behind wealth and comfort to seek meaning in a world of suffering. Even the minimal effort it takes to mail it in, to quietly quit, feels beyond me—the performance too exhausting to maintain.

The Buddha once left behind a palace. I’m just trying to leave behind a brand deck.

So I slowly disentangle myself from the life I’ve built, unweaving the tapestry thread by careful thread. I sell the car that sits unused most days, give up the garage that costs as much as an apartment in some cities, take fewer and fewer remote gigs that pay well but hollow out my soul, learn to live with less, and, in the emptying, discover space for something new to grow.

Days unfold differently now, shaped by purpose rather than profit. I teach mindfulness to parolees from Rikers in a halfway house on Monday evenings, their faces initially skeptical, then gradually softening as they discover inner resources they never knew they had. I help run the Buddhist group on Tuesdays in a rented room that smells of incense and possibility, volunteer at an afterschool program where children’s laughter heals something ancient in me, mentor recovering addicts who recognize in my eyes that I’ve walked through the same fire. The pay is minimal, some days nonexistent. But this new life and sense of self nourishes me in ways my old salary never could, like comparing fast food to a meal cooked with love. I’m building connections that run deep, creating a web of relationships based on something real, not the transactional exchanges of my former life. When people ask what I do now, I stumble at first, unsure how to explain what a Buddhist teacher is in a world obsessed with titles and status. “I try to help others find out who else they can be,” I might say, the words feeling both inadequate and exactly right. But the truth is, I’m really finding that out for myself, day by surprising day.

I’ve built my life around who I thought I was—identity as a fortress against uncertainty. My job title. My relationship status. My political views. A social media presence carefully curated to reflect a person who doesn’t actually exist. I’m the musical one in my friend group, the creative strategist, brand storyteller, good neighbor, progressive with the right opinions at the right times. These labels feel solid, comforting, familiar as old furniture. But what happens when they suddenly don’t fit anymore? When the chair breaks under your weight?

Imagine waking up one morning and feeling like a stranger to yourself, your reflection in the mirror a person you barely recognize. It happens. Sometimes gradually, like a tide coming in, sometimes all at once like a lightning strike. The ancients knew about this—they called it different things in different tongues. Around 500 BCE, great philosophers—Heraclitus, Laozi, the Buddha—emerged who all pointed to the same truth: Clinging to what is unreliable causes suffering as surely as night follows day.

I remember my first heartbreak—the feeling of “who am I without them?” My identity was so wrapped up in being someone’s partner that separation felt like amputation. That was a tiny taste of ego death. But this goes deeper. Much deeper than romantic loss.

I think about what I tell myself in the mirror each morning, mantras so familiar they’ve become invisible: “I’m creative.” “I’m bad with numbers.” “I’ll never have a healthy relationship.” These feel like facts etched in stone, don’t they? But they’re just stories, narratives written in invisible ink. Stories that help me make sense of my life, sure. And they boost my confidence when they’re positive, a warm hand on the shoulder. Maybe the harsh, self-critical views can provide us with excuses when we’re struggling to meet our expectations—shields against trying and failing.

In those spaces between my old self and whatever comes next—that’s where ego death happens. It can feel like free-falling through empty space without a parachute. Terrifying. Disorienting. Like being lost in a city where I don’t speak the language, signs meaningless, no map to guide me home.

But here’s a secret whispered by those who’ve made the journey: It can also feel like freedom. Indigenous cultures created rituals for this—vision quests where young people stepped outside their known selves to discover something larger than individual identity, returning transformed. In the 1960s, a generation turned to psychedelics to break free from society’s rigid boxes, seeking authentic experience beyond social conditioning. Today, people travel to foreign countries where no one knows their name or history, dive into therapy that questions core beliefs, or join spiritual communities seeking the same transformation—death preceding rebirth.

Some try to speed up the process. Psychedelics can blast open the gates of perception like dynamite opening a sealed cave, overwhelming the brain with unfiltered sensory input that bypasses ordinary consciousness. Suddenly, the boundaries between me and everything else dissolve like salt in water. I merge with the universe, stars pulsing with my heartbeat. I disappear completely yet paradoxically feel more present than ever before.

It sounds mystical, doesn’t it? Sometimes it is—glimpses of something larger than words can contain. People return with profound insights—greater compassion flowing naturally, deeper connection to nature that transforms their relationship to the environment, less concern about status and money that once seemed so important. But these insights fade without integration, like dreams upon waking. Without practice. The old patterns creep back in when Monday morning arrives with its demands and expectations, the ordinary world reasserting itself.

And the forced approach comes with risks not mentioned in breathless articles about transformative experiences. What feels like enlightenment for one person might trigger paranoia or panic in another, psychic trapdoors opening unexpectedly. Especially if I’m predisposed to certain mental health conditions, the plunge can become a dangerous free fall without a safety net.

Buddhism offers a gentler path, less dramatic but perhaps more sustainable. Instead of tearing down my self-concept all at once like demolishing a building, I learn to see through it gradually, brick by transparent brick. Like slowly adjusting my eyes to darkness rather than being thrown into a pitch-black room and told to find my way. With various meditation and visualization practices undertaken day after patient day, I begin to notice how everything I take to be “me”—my body with its aches and pleasures, my feelings that rise and fall like waves, my thoughts that appear from nowhere like birds crossing the sky—is constantly changing, never static. Nothing stays the same from one moment to the next, not even the cells of my body or the neurons firing in my brain. There’s no solid core to grasp on to, no unchanging essence that defines me.

The ego doesn’t disappear in some dramatic explosion, a spiritual fireworks display. It becomes transparent, seen for what it always was—a useful fiction, a convenient shorthand, necessary but not ultimate. Like realizing the glass barrier I’ve been pressing against was never there at all, the limitation imaginary. Some days I’ll still cling to my labels and roles out of habit or fear. That’s OK. I’m human, navigating a world built on these conventions. But increasingly, I hold them lightly in open palms rather than clenched fists. I see them as helpful tools rather than absolute truths—maps but not the territory. When life inevitably changes, as it always does, I won’t shatter along with my old identity but flow like water finding a new channel to the sea.

The post Ego Death on 9/11 appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.

articles.title: Penchants of the polymaths
articles.summary: The fathers of Islamic science hold lessons for students: breadth over specialisation, and never let constraints get in the way - by Mariam Sabri Read on Aeon

articles.title: Boulder proposes ending free recreation access for low-income residents
articles.summary: The proposed 2027 budget includes cuts to pool hours and fitness and childcare programs, while also scaling back a program that provides free access for low-income residents. The post Boulder proposes ending free recreation access for low-i…
articles.content:
Boulder residents who currently qualify for free access to city recreation facilities would have to pay 25% of the cost next year under proposed changes to Parks and Recreation’s financial aid program.

The proposed cuts would also shorten Scott Carpenter Pool’s season by four weeks, reduce indoor pool hours, offer fewer drop-in fitness classes and eliminate child care at East Boulder Community Center.

The changes are part of the city’s proposed 2027 budget, which seeks to close a projected $6.3 million General Fund gap.

Planned changes for Parks and Recreation in 2027 include reducing the number of drop-in fitness classes. The city said the reductions are based on participation, time of day and overlap with other offerings. Nonresidents currently pay a 15% premium for fitness classes. The premium would increase to 20% next year. 

In addition to shortening Scott Carpenter Pool’s season, the proposal would reduce indoor pool hours before Memorial Day and after Labor Day, when the city says use is lower.

“While people love it, the visitation does not equal what it costs to actually operate the facility,” said Ali Rhodes, director of Parks and Recreation, referring to Scott Carpenter Pool.

The child watch program at the East Boulder Community Center, which offers child care while a parent or guardian uses the facility, would be eliminated. The service would remain available at the North Boulder Rec Center. 

Qualifying low-income residents currently receive free access to city rec facilities. Under the proposal, the city would cover 75% of the cost in 2027, leaving participants to pay the remaining 25%. A 50% discount of up to $500 per year for certain rec programs for low-income residents would continue. 

Parks and Recreation, which relies heavily on sales tax revenue and service charges, has seen revenue remain mostly flat since 2014, while labor, utility and equipment costs have risen, according to city officials. The department is also facing increased use of its financial aid program without a sustainable funding source to meet growing demand, according to a recent city staff memo. The department provided about $930,000 in financial aid in 2025, covering approximately 77,000 facility visits. Subsidy costs are projected to reach $1.2 million in 2026. 

Parks and Recreation’s proposed budget for 2027 is $37.1 million, which would be used to maintain 86 parks and plazas, 42 playgrounds, three rec centers and 1,800 acres of natural areas. That is up slightly from $36.5 million in 2026. 

Rhodes has warned that 2027 reductions will be noticeable, in part because the department has already exhausted savings that do not affect services. 

The department is already struggling to operate Spruce Pool, with no city funding allocated beyond 2027. The pool is beloved by local swimmers who prefer a calmer, less competitive environment, but draws fewer visitors and therefore less revenue than the larger Scott Carpenter Pool. 

The department is not planning any significant changes to rec center or pool passes for city residents. Last year, the city began charging residents more for passes that provide access to both rec centers and pools. Previously, a single pass included access to both. 

Jackson Hite, senior manager of business services for Parks and Recreation, said visitation has flattened in 2026 compared with 2025 and 2024. Projected visitation growth for 2028 also appears to be “modest,” Hite said. 

A proposed bond measure, headed to Boulder’s ballot this November, could indirectly relieve pressure on Parks and Recreation’s budget. The measure, known as the Recreation and Safety Bond, would allow Boulder to borrow $400 million to tackle the city’s maintenance backlog. The debt would be repaid through an annual property tax. The measure does not specify exactly how the money would be spent, but the city has said it intends to use the funds for projects such as the $65 million replacement of the South Boulder Rec Center and $72 million for maintenance at the North Boulder Rec Center and relocation of the West Age Well Center.

While funds from the measure cannot be used for day-to-day operations, Rhodes expects that addressing the maintenance backlog would create more flexibility for existing funds. 

“We do expect to see some efficiency in the operating budgets because of the significant amount we are spending on reactive repair,” Rhodes said. According to city staff, Boulder spends $11 per square foot to maintain deteriorating buildings, compared with an industry standard of $5 per square foot to maintain buildings in good condition.

The post Boulder proposes ending free recreation access for low-income residents appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

articles.title: Whose AI Will Rule The World?
articles.summary: The post Whose AI Will Rule The World? appeared first on NOEMA.
articles.content:
“What appears to humanity as the history of capitalism is an invasion from the future by an artificial intelligent space that must assemble itself entirely from its enemy’s resources.“
—Nick Land

SHANGHAI — Today, China and the United States are co-creating a powerful new technology that changes how we think, communicate with each other and understand what consciousness itself means. Some compare it to the invention of fire, or electricity. But a more apt analogy might be the invention of writing: a system that both liberates our thoughts — and constrains them.

When did civilization, as a collective archive of thoughts put down into writing, first begin? Do those beginnings encode certain tendencies into the users of language today, whether those using the language are aware of it or not? Our world has two dominating cultural source codes: one from the West, however construed, and the other that began in Yinxu, Henan, around 3,500 years ago, where the written Chinese language emerged in the form of prophetic oracle bones. Scholars like Yuri Pines have long argued that the ideographic nature of the Chinese script was the primary engine of its cultural continuity.

Take 文, the root word for writing, literature, culture, civilization. The oracle bone inscription was of a person’s body, undergoing a painful ritual transformation of tattooing or scarification. Originally, the word meant “interlocking patterns.” And that is what the Chinese language and civilization form: a huge mental map of interlocking patterns. The written Chinese language is what makes China, China.

Today, the dominant mechanism by which information is transmitted in China is transitioning from the Chinese language to digital networks that communicate in binary or qubits. Paradoxically, this algorithmic form of consciousness is deeply compatible with the traditional Chinese civilizational source code. The concept of an individual being part of a larger network of thought and action transitions seamlessly into the digital age. A civilization whose thinking has always been about the optimized, visual juxtaposition of concepts finds its ultimate realization in the neural network.

Language And The Origins Of The Chinese State

You Shou (1906–1994) was a prominent Chinese archaeologist and master calligrapher. She argued that the oracle bone script (jiaguwen) and the bronze inscriptions (jinwen) were intrinsically linked to the materials that were used to make them: the bones, the human labor, the metal, the climate. The Chinese characters emerged from the Chinese people and the Chinese landscape; the people and the land predated the words, and the words described and sought to control the people and the land, in a literal sense. 

You’s theories linked the development of character stroke structures to the physical tools, labor and materials (bone, bronze, stone) used by ancient peoples: The act of writing was the consummation in and about Yinxu, the place where they were developed, from a hierarchical social structure to the work of the workers who provided the bones and metal in the first place. The evolution of Chinese characters, You wrote, tracks China’s development as a society, with new ways of seeing literally inscribed in the language. Recent examples would be Japanese loan words like zhuyi (主义, “ism”) or jingji (经济, “economy”), or new compound words like diannao (电脑), which means computer. By analyzing character structures, she traced changes in early Chinese geography, social organization and ancient ritual practices. The words, she thought, were invented as a way to answer questions about the order of the cosmos.

The oracle bones were a little like a Ouija board; the person preparing them did not know the outcome in advance. The priest or diviner would pose a question, usually to the high god Di or the ancestors, then apply heat to ox shoulder blades or turtle shells. Shang scribes routinely split a single question for the spirits into positive and negative outcomes: It will rain tomorrow or It will not rain tomorrow. Heated, the bone would crack and the holy man would read a response to his question. Auspicious divine answers, dates and consequences would be recorded on the bones. The Shang had intense self-doubt; they couldn’t go to war or plant crops without performing rituals to check in with God. The priests, surrounded as they were by the stench of blood and bone, asked God: What is going to happen to us?

And yet, much as the story of Adam and Eve is about forbidden knowledge, the Shang didn’t think of God as telling them these things; what they were doing was more like eavesdropping on divine knowledge. They lived in a world where all of human life was enveloped in the safety of ritual. But by using oracle bones to solve trivial, anxious survival puzzles, they accidentally built the infrastructure of the Chinese mind: assigning an unalterable, concept-driven visual symbol to a natural phenomenon. It was an act of cosmic taming. They were bringing the terrifying, unpredictable movements of ancestors, rivers and seasons into a stable, legible linguistic architecture. Like today’s five-year plans, the oracle bones were not economic forecasts; they were magical, state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence.

These archaic concepts shape the language of Chinese statecraft today. For example, 盟 or alliance, which is used to describe the European Union and ASEAN, consists of a bowl or vessel (皿) at the bottom topped by the character for bright or clear (明), which originally depicted a window illuminated by the moon or by a sacrificial fire. In ancient times, to seal a political pact, lords dug a pit, slaughtered a sacrificial animal (often a bull or dog), cut off its left ear and caught the blood in a bronze vessel (皿). The lords smeared raw blood on their lips and swore an oath to the gods (明). The 盟 character thus physically encodes the wet, copper flavor of shared blood that bound ancient factions together.

Yinxu was, some say, a city of perhaps 150,000 people, and had no physical walls but was sharply divided by class. The Shang elite lived in a state of ritualistic intoxication. Occupying grand palaces, they spent their days hunting big game on the Henan plains (elephants, rhinoceroses and tigers still roamed the warm, humid landscape); drinking vast quantities of warm, herb-infused wine from heavy bronze jue vessels; and conducting military raids on neighboring tribes. Their entire psychological reality was geared toward validating their lineage through conspicuous feasting and violence.

Shang craftsmen, meanwhile, enjoyed a privileged, middle-tier status, protected by the state because they produced the technology of power. In industrial quarters like Xiaomintun, they operated massive, hyper-coordinated bronze foundries. The vast majority of the population were ordinary peasants whose lives were grindingly hard. They did not live in houses; they lived in pits dug into the earth and covered by rough timber and thatch roofs to shield them from the freezing winters. 

Aside from bronze, Yinxu’s largest industry was bone tool production. In a single workshop site, archaeologists uncovered millions of discarded animal bones (primarily cattle, pig and deer) that had been systematically carved into arrows, hairpins and awls. The city must have smelled of boiled animal fat, charcoal smoke and raw marrow. When a king died, or when a major palace foundation was laid, hundreds of human beings were systematically executed to serve as structural or spiritual filler. Captured prisoners were bound, decapitated or dismembered by the dozens, their heads buried in neat, geometric rows in the palace plazas to appease the high god Di and the royal ancestors. To keep the world from collapsing, the Shang kings had to unleash torrents of human blood, torch bones with fire and mobilize hundreds of thousands of hands to dig earth and melt bronze.

I first learned of You Shou while researching the history of the Cultural Revolution in Harbin. She was at the center of a group called the “eight weirdos,” Harbin scholars who were singled out for torment by Red Guards who were trying to eradicate the “four olds,” (四旧): old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits. The Communist project had to crush scholars like You Shou because her work revealed that the Party was not a radical break from the past, but an unwitting captive of it. The uncanny image of a hierarchical and violent Chinese elite who used semi-mystical techniques to conjure a future into being was too uncomfortable, heresy to the notion of a New China.

None of the great ethicists of ancient Chinese culture — Confucius, Laozi and friends — lived in Yinxu. All of that came later. But the invention of language was a prerequisite to their work. 

The conclusion might be that today, as the world stumbles terrified into future climate change and cultural decadence, that sometimes, the sacrifices work. The AI being built is not a good in itself; the questions we ask it may be as trivial as the Shang asking the oracle bones what part of the forest was a good place to hunt. But the platform created may birth systems, ideas and thoughts which we cannot currently imagine, in formats that exceed our wildest dreams. That’s what happened to the Shang, anyway.

The Scientific Sovereign

For the past few months, I’ve been corresponding with Pan Jianwei, China’s quantum computing champion, trying to understand his views on how Chinese science fits into the world and what the significance of quantum computing will be for China’s future. Pan’s adviser, Anton Zeilinger, won the Nobel Prize in physics in 2022. Working in Zeilinger’s lab, Pan was part of the elite team that achieved the world’s first experimental demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1997. When Zeilinger asked Pan what his long-term dream was, Pan famously replied: “To build a world-class quantum physics lab in China.” By 2016, Pan had become the mastermind behind Micius, a satellite that enables quantum communication across vast distances. Pan is largely seen as one of China’s most likely candidates for the Nobel. But China has bigger fish to fry.

Quantum computing replaces the traditional language by which computers organize information with a new way, our understanding of which originated with Albert Einstein’s theories. While classical computers rely on binary logic — processing information through rigid transistors as individual bits that must be strictly a 0 or a 1 — quantum computing uses qubits. Qubits are particles that exist based on two seemingly contradictory concepts: superposition and entanglement. Superposition means a qubit can exist in multiple states simultaneously — a complex, fluid blend of both 0 and 1 at the same time. Entanglement is a unique connection where qubits become linked, allowing a change in one to instantly dictate the state of another.

By manipulating these fluid probabilities rather than processing data step by step, a quantum computer can map out massive, complex solution spaces all at once. In this sense, quantum computing is to computing what Chinese characters are to the Roman alphabet: Both apparently fulfill the same function, but the way in which they do so is radically different.

In recent months, the White House has been tweeting about quantum supremacy alongside the usual half-baked AI-generated images; in the 2025 National Security Strategy, quantum is mentioned, along with AI and biotech, as a field that the U.S. must not cede to rivals like China. It’s seen as important because if China breaks through on quantum computing, it’ll have a way around traditional public-key encryption and be able to read all of America’s secrets.

Although he is increasingly prominent in China’s political ecosystem, Pan is not a member of the Communist Party. His allegiance lies with the Jiusan Society, one of China’s eight legally sanctioned political parties. Rather than being elevated to an administrative role like, for example, Chen Jining, the environmental scientist turned Shanghai party secretary, Pan continues to manage his quantum lab in Hefei. In a China increasingly more interested in social development through advanced computation rather than human resources, that position might be equally powerful — and a lot more fun. Instead of wasting time navigating the standard, hyper-competitive and granular grant application cycles that consume Western researchers, Pan just gets large sums of money transferred into his jurisdiction. Under Xi Jinping’s mandate for absolute “sci-tech self-reliance,” Pan’s operational authority means that if he identifies a critical bottleneck, the state quickly funnels funding and manpower directly to him. 

His work and influence extend far beyond university walls to the commercial monetization of his discoveries. QuantumCTek was founded by his academic research team, for example. In a massive vote of confidence, China Telecom acquired a 23% stake in the firm to build out unhackable national communications infrastructure based directly on Pan’s proprietary hardware. In this sense, Pan exemplifies a new class in China: politically untouchable, trusted enough to receive a blank check for funding and proactively supported in commercialization by state-owned entities.

In an email to me, Pan shared five pages of thoughts of his own and other quantum scientists in China. In short, he said, China’s government believes that technological change creates economic change creates political change. It also believes that the world is on the brink of a technological revolution driven by AI, quantum computing, biotech, new energy sources, materials science and other fields. In the tradition of the Shang, the Chinese are ready to make any sacrifice, as long as the new language that is being created is one they understand. 

As Hong Ding, a Chinese Academy of Sciences academician, put it in an email to me:

Basic science … expands, revises or deepens our understanding of the laws and mechanisms themselves. It asks a question whose answer we genuinely do not know, and — this is the part that never stops surprising me — the answer, pursued for its own sake, later reshapes the world.

A New Golden Age?

Michael Kratsios is an alumnus of arguably the two most forward-looking incubators of science policy in the world today: Thiel Capital and Tsinghua University. Today, he is Trump’s science adviser. In his report on reforming American science, which he presents as being the biggest revision to American science policy since Vannevar Bush’s postwar “Science: The Endless Frontier,” we see one of the most concrete and detailed indications yet that the Trump administration is adopting Chinese mechanisms, inspired by a close and meticulous study of what makes the Chinese model successful. 

Kratsios likely wouldn’t admit it, but his report represents a fundamental shift away from the traditional, decentralized Western model of free academic inquiry toward a centralized, mission-driven, state-backed system that mirrors Beijing’s tech-governance model. For example, echoing a long-time Thiel idea, the report fiercely critiques traditional, consensus-driven Western academic peer-review boards as sluggish and conservative; by definition, peer review means that new ideas must be checked by the gatekeepers of the old. Kratsios proposes a “broader menu of selection mechanisms,” specifically introducing “golden tickets” that empower individual, state-appointed reviewers to unilaterally fund highly ambitious, high-risk proposals without consensus approval. That’s exactly what high-flyer scientists like Pan Jianwei have: They’ve earned the trust of the system and are treated as partners in a venture capital fund.

The centerpieces of the Kratsios report are the “Genesis Mission” and a newly funded National Science Foundation initiative called “X-Labs.” These are explicitly structured as “Manhattan Project-style” efforts designed to build highly focused, multidisciplinary independent research organizations that apply AI directly to accelerated scientific productivity, totally bypassing legacy academic boundaries. Kratsios is effectively recreating the structure of China’s National Laboratories and State Key Laboratories (such as Pan Jianwei’s quantum facilities in Hefei or Fudan University’s Xuemin Institute, itself modeled on the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton).

But even if the U.S. adopts many Chinese methods, it lacks the critical ingredient of Chinese science success: Chinese people. Lots of them. Effectively, Kratsios is proposing to make up for this gap by letting AI, a “country of geniuses in a datacenter” as Dario Amodei once put it, do for America what millions of Chinese STEM graduates do for China.

Democratic critics (like Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California) have explicitly denounced this policy, noting that the administration “has been systematically destroying the U.S. science enterprise.” Dan Wang and Julian Gewirtz criticized Trump policies in The New York Times for emulating China, particularly the proactive way that the Pentagon is seeking to supervise Anthropic, which they allege is a direct copy of China’s state capitalism.

Beijing doesn’t nationalize tech firms; it integrates the state into private enterprises. But to be fair to Kratsios, China’s science structure is clearly working, and the degree of integration between policymakers, fundamental research (in fields like materials science or chemistry), burgeoning fields (like batteries) and global domination of supply chains, can feel new. The Thiel wing of the Trump administration is seeking truth from facts. The questions for Americans are: Is the overall strategy of rivaling Chinese scale effects via AI likely to work? And: As we pursue these processes, how will our own society change? Are we comfortable with that?

In 2014, Thiel wrote in his tech-founder bible “Zero to One” that China is a society characterized by definite pessimism: The Chinese believe that tragic disaster lurks, so they make comprehensive plans to avoid it. In contrast, American society of the Vannevar Bush era (the 1950s) was one of definite optimism: America made plans because it believed that the future was bright. These outlooks don’t neatly map onto countries today (if they ever did), but if anything, as AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans.

The Silicon Valley radicals adjacent to Thiel — and therefore the White House — have been making provocative remarks about science for some time. For example, Curtis Yarvin recently asserted that NASA was founded by Nazis who’d gone to Alabama. Yarvin’s claim rests entirely on the historical reality of Operation Paperclip, the American mission to relocate top German scientists and engineers to the U.S. during the final stages of World War II. China today resembles the U.S. then: an industrial superpower that senses it is not quite as sophisticated as the decadent power it wishes to replace. From this vantage point, Kratsios (a former instructor at Tsinghua who knows what the Chinese are thinking as well as any American government official) doesn’t want the U.S. to be eclipsed. 

The Chinese AI policy that American policymakers like Kratsios are inspired by proceeds with great clarity: There is a list of problems and AI is being used systematically to solve those problems. The Chinese assume that private companies and new technologies that depend on government support and the participation and consent of the population should serve that population. And as with the rest of their products, what happens in China doesn’t stay in China, but is exported to whoever will take it, which increasingly means the Global South.

When AI Runs The World

Not long ago, I was invited to Nanning, the capital of Guangxi Province, a three-hour train ride from Shenzhen but culturally a backwater. The Chinese five-year plans allocate different tasks to different regions: Big cities like Beijing and Shanghai are for capital-heavy innovation and research, which Guangxi is positioned to disseminate to Southeast Asia. Inside the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center, a digital display advertised different AI applications: agriculture, logistics, public safety, manufacturing, local finance, healthcare and education. China invites leaders from Vietnam, Laos and Indonesia to this place and says: Look, we figured out how to use AI to make our farmers richer, our factories better, our streets safer. We can do that for you too.

Nanning itself felt like a display of what Chinese style development could bring. Technically, this is the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with ethnic minorities such as the Zhuang dominating. Signs on government buildings are bilingual. Nanning’s nominal GDP per capita sits at nearly $10,000, double Vietnam’s and nearly five times higher than in Laos or Cambodia. And the infrastructure, public safety and general atmosphere is excellent. So the vibe of the AI center was very much showing off: All this could be yours. Sign on the dotted line.

The Chinese government’s AI+ plan focuses on applications in sectors that the government has a role in and often in places where the population can’t afford what others can (high-quality education, healthcare, etc.). AI is understood as a tool, or perhaps a commodity like electricity, and the Chinese plan is to use that tool to solve Chinese problems — reducing the cost of electricity, safeguarding the country’s food supply, providing national healthcare via AI-driven medical solutions. China’s civilization, patriarchal and authoritarian though it may be, has a clear goal in mind: make Chinese people safer, richer, stronger and, ultimately, more Chinese.

At the recent World AI Conference in Shanghai, I saw an ancient Chinese scroll painting underneath a fancy screen made by CamScanner. The proximity of the pair seemed to underline the message that Chinese tech companies are expected to serve Chinese civilizational needs — as defined by the government. Even when this feels like an afterthought, it’s politically important for Chinese AI companies to symbolically pledge allegiance to their country’s heritage.

That’s them; American civilization is different. Many aspects of the Chinese model would not fly in America. Surveillance, for example. Look at the backlash to Flock. A government that makes decisions for individuals without asking for their permission is, generally, an unwelcome idea in the States.

But Americans need not adopt any of China’s specific solutions to ask the important questions: What is AI actually doing for Americans? Is the general population in control, or are the Silicon Valley oligarchs? And which system — China’s state-directed planning or America’s obviously eroded democratic capitalism — will be more universally acceptable over the long term? 

The post Whose AI Will Rule The World? appeared first on NOEMA.

articles.title: You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work
articles.summary: Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequent…
articles.content:
Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

Rustout vs. burnout

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”

These people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another said, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”

Why don’t we talk about rustout?

Rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person said, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”

It’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person said.

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”

How rustout arises

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly important for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”

Naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

What to do if you are rusting out

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

That is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

articles.title: The Metta of Mister Rogers
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after his last episode aired, Gayathri Narayanan reflects on Fred Rogers’ enduring practice of loving-kindness, acceptance, and seeing the good in others. The post The Metta of Mister Rogers appeared first on Lion’s Roar.
articles.content:
“Love isn’t a state of perfect caring. It is an active noun like struggle.”
—Fred Rogers

This year, August 31st marks twenty-five years since the last episode of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood aired. Growing up outside of the United States, I wasn’t exposed to Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood as a child. I first registered who Fred Rogers was when I saw Tom Hanks play him in the 2019 film A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood, through which I began to understand how much of an impact he had in American households, offering a daily dose of goodness through the television.

I watched the 2018 documentary film about his life, Won’t You Be My Neighbor?, for the first time only recently. I was moved watching him interact with children in real time, not as an actor or puppeteer, but simply talking to a child, looking at each one as if they were the most important person he could possibly be speaking to.

“He was asking us to be there for our neighbors, to reach out in small ways to whoever happens to be in front of us, and ultimately make them part of our neighborhood.”

In one scene, a ten-year-old boy named Jeff Erlanger, who was in a wheelchair after spinal surgery, sat across from Rogers. He asked him quite directly about his wheelchair, why he used it, and what it was like. There was no discomfort in the way he approached him. The message was the same one he offered children over and over again: you don’t need to change anything about yourself to be loved. Then the two of them sang “It’s You I Like” together. I found it so sweet and moving to watch, thinking about what it must be like for a child to have somebody look at them that way, as if they were completely accepted just as they were.

As I watched, the word that kept coming to mind was metta. Metta is usually translated as loving-kindness, a kind of unconditional friendliness and goodwill toward ourselves and others. Every time he looks straight into the camera and speaks to the children watching at home, it’s as if he’s actually seeing you with eyes of unconditional love and acceptance. He reminds us that you don’t have to accomplish something, look a certain way, get the right grades, or become somebody special before you are loved. There’s something innately good and lovable about you already.

Rogers was famously criticized by some conservative commentators for this, accused of helping raise a generation of entitled children who thought they were wonderful without having to earn it, but that’s not how I see it. Rogers was an ordained Presbyterian minister and a deeply spiritual person. He wasn’t trying to pump up children’s egos. He was speaking, I think, from a belief in the inherent sacredness — or basic goodness — of every being.

I try to do some version of this in my own work. Whatever a person comes to me with, whether a physical, mental, or emotional struggle, I try to see beyond what I sometimes think of as the externality of the person. I try to see something core in them that is good and whole, beyond all the quirks and neuroses of personality. When I can do that, something changes in the relationship, but it’s something I have to remind myself of. It isn’t simply a state I inhabit all the time.

When I first encountered Rogers through the Tom Hanks film, my reaction was that he seemed like a yogi, someone who simply embodied love and compassion. It looked effortless, as though that was just who he was. In reality, things were more complicated, as the documentary explained. Rogers had been a frequently ill child who was bullied. His beloved puppet, Daniel Striped Tiger, became a kind of alter ego, a way for him to express his own fear, insecurity, and vulnerability.

As Thich Nhat Hanh’s famous teaching goes, “No mud, no lotus.” The mud of Rogers’ own suffering seems to have become part of what allowed something very beautiful to grow. He could have become bitter or angry from what he experienced as a child. Instead, he seemed determined not to inflict that same pain on somebody else.

That doesn’t mean it all came naturally. Rogers swam a mile most mornings. He weighed himself every day, having been called “fat Freddy” by his childhood bullies. He studied at seminary. He had routines and disciplines. When he stopped making the show for a period, his wife recalled that he seemed to lose something of his sense of purpose.

People who knew Rogers’ television persona often wondered the same thing I found myself wondering when I first encountered him: Is this guy actually real? Is he like this when the camera is off? By all accounts, the answer was yes. “Mr. Rogers” wasn’t simply a character he played on television — it was how he tried to live.

One of the most powerful scenes from the show came in 1969, when Rogers invited François Clemmons, a Black cast member who played Officer Clemmons, to sit beside him and cool his feet in the same small wading pool. This was at a time when segregated swimming pools were still very much part of American life. Afterwards, Rogers dried Clemmons’ feet. It was, in its own way, quite subversive. He wasn’t particularly subtle about what he wanted to say.

Yet Clemmons was also gay, but Rogers asked him to keep that private because he feared the controversy could cost the program its audience. Though it was likely to protect a show he thought could do a lot of good, there were limits to what even Fred Rogers was willing to take on in that moment, and there was a real cost to Clemmons in being asked to remain closeted. 

Rogers wasn’t some godlike person beyond human struggle. He was a human being trying, within the constraints of his time and his own limitations, to approach the world from a place of compassion, faith, and love. 

He was also, in some ways, an activist. He just had a very different way of doing it. You see that in his famous 1969 Senate testimony defending funding for public television. He had prepared a speech, but didn’t really use it. He simply talked about what he was trying to do for children and why he believed it mattered. The senator listening to him was visibly disarmed and finally told him, in effect, that he’d earned the twenty million dollars he was asking Congress to preserve. There was great conviction in Fred Rogers’ quietness.

The last new episode of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood aired only eleven days before September 11, 2001. About a year later, his producers persuaded a reluctant Rogers to return to the studio to record messages for parents. He wasn’t sure he had anything adequate to say. My sense was that the scale of what had happened shook him. The message he eventually gave was one of hope. He invoked the idea of tikkun olam, from the Jewish faith, which he rendered as a call for all of us, whatever our particular work, to become “repairers of creation.”

Rogers himself would not have called any of this metta. He would perhaps have understood what he was offering through the language of grace and God’s unconditional love, which isn’t quite the same claim metta makes. In the Christian understanding, you are worthy of God’s love because you are a child of God. Metta begins somewhere different, as a practice. We deliberately cultivate goodwill toward ourselves, then toward people we love, and gradually extend it outward toward more and more beings.

My own roots are in the Hindu philosophy of Advaita Vedanta, and that may be why these different ways of speaking about love don’t feel so far apart to me. Advaita points toward a reality in which the separation between “me” and “you” is ultimately not as solid as we imagine it. The practice of metta can soften those boundaries, too. As the heart opens to wider and wider circles of beings, the world begins to feel less divided into us and them. For me, these traditions point toward something universally recognizable: a love that excludes no one.

I think that’s part of why many people find themselves crying watching Mr. Rogers all these years later, myself included. There’s a grief in watching the world Rogers created in his neighborhood — a kind of grief for what could be. I wish we could have that kind of world, I found myself thinking.

He wasn’t asking us to fix the whole world — he was asking us to be there for our neighbors, to reach out in small ways to whoever happens to be in front of us, and ultimately make them part of our neighborhood. We don’t have to solve everything. Tending to our own little corner of the world matters. The quality of attention is part of what metta looks like when it leaves the cushion.

Fred Rogers kept repeating a version of the same thing throughout his life: I like you as you are. Reach out to your neighbor, he taught us. Respond to the needs of whoever shows up in front of you. Slow down enough to actually see them. Twenty-five years after his last episode aired, his message still feels like a practice worth learning. 

The post The Metta of Mister Rogers appeared first on Lion’s Roar.

articles.title: DD403 / In praise of ‘it depends’
articles.summary: Issue 403: In praise of ‘it depends’ – Read the full issue in the archive.
articles.content:
If you’ve been reasonably lucky with your education, aren’t mentally overburdened, and haven’t stopped being curious about other people, something interesting can happen as you get older: your views become less absolute. With every decade of lived experience, I’m collecting more shades of grey, and discovering more holes in the neat explanations that once made sense of my world.

Rebecca Solnit’s latest essay is excellent company for that work. She describes our human tendency to oversimplify complex realities and the many mental shortcuts we use to arrive at tidy conclusions. It’s a piece I wish everyone would read at least once.

We seem to allow less room to wonder, doubt, improvise, or simply admit we don’t know. (See also ‘knowingness’ in DD333.) Solnit describes this pressure as feeling “naked without an opinion”, where confidence and certainty can matter more than having the facts first.

It often looks like this: declaring something a complete success or a total failure, looking for evidence that supports the story we already believe, or treating a diverse group of people as though they were one person with one opinion.

“Categories too often become where thought goes to die. That is, there’s a widespread tendency to act as if once something has been categorized, no further consideration is required.”

From airtight categories come blanket statements: climate action is too late, protest is pointless, voting doesn’t matter. These statements sound like facts but function as an excuse to stop paying attention. Reality is almost always layered and often contradictory:

“We cannot save everything but that does not mean we cannot save anything; we have solutions that though spectacular are not perfect; no one solution can do it all so while there is no solution there are many solutions that must be pursued together; there are heroes and villains and some governments are both at once.”

Solnit isn’t arguing that everything is ambiguous, or that there are never clear answers. Quite the opposite. Context can sometimes reveal a truth that a supposedly ‘neutral’ presentation obscures. ‘Natural’ disasters make more sense when connected to climate change. Violence against women makes more sense when we recognise its systemic patterns. And sometimes a comfortable middle ground can disguise a difficult truth:

“One piece of that is the idea that centrism and the status quo are neutral ground when they’re often either the acceptance of whatever inequality and oppression has long existed, which results in treating the pursuit of equality and rights as acts of aggression. Or it’s the idea that truth is somewhere in the middle as if there’s some halfway measure between truth and lies, human rights and human rights abuses.”

Living with infinite greys will very likely make you an annoyance to anyone certain about a category of people, an event or an opinion. To them it reads like having no firm views of your own, but false certainty has done far more damage than ‘it depends’ ever has.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai
