articles.title: A New Kind Of Creative Poverty
articles.summary: The post A New Kind Of Creative Poverty appeared first on NOEMA.
articles.content:
Editor’s Note: Noema is transparent about AI use in its pieces. We publish original human-generated ideas but allow authorized, disclosed use of AI in certain cases. Please see details at the end of this piece.

During a dark stretch of Covid, I dove into Joan Didion’s “The Year of Magical Thinking,” her book about processing her husband’s death. Didion wrote that she could not give away his shoes. She had managed the suits, the shirts, the jackets. But when she got to the shoes, she paused: “I stood there for a moment, then realized why: he would need shoes if he was to return.”

I was living in solitude in an apartment recently emptied by a long-term relationship. When the rental lease lapsed, I renewed it and renewed it again, keeping the furniture exactly as it had been, the lamp at the same angle. What Didion was dealing with was, in Orwell’s words,  “the recognizable experiences of human beings.” Through her writing, I felt relief wash over me as I suddenly saw my own stalled life right under my nose.

What many readers come to Didion for — what I went to her for — is the record of a mind at work on its own chaos, a way of processing thought, of handling the formless weather in the head. I love watching her spill it all out, like discovering the neighbors’ house is total chaos, and feeling assured that no one’s life is truly put-together.

Being gripped by the experiences evoked by writers like Didion could be a survival trait, shaped over countless years of evolution. The psychologist Bruce Hood argues that we are a self-domesticated species: Over roughly a thousand generations, human beings have favored cooperation and sociability as traits in our mates and allies. In doing so, we rewired our brains to read, track, mimic and crave other minds. We have been self-domesticating, Hood writes, “through the invention of culture and practices that ensure that we can live together,” and eventually win the evolution game. To be gripped by another person’s inner life is old equipment built into us.

Social media is a product of this ancient urge, a machine for exercising our interest in other humans at a scale evolution never planned for. But what happens when we learn that this other human, or this “recognizable experience,” has been artificially generated by an LLM? Maybe this is why the counterfeit cuts the way it does. AI slop feels like betrayal. There is this haunting feeling when you lean toward a face and then find only a mask, with no person behind it.

And this feeling is probably one reason people have become obsessed with running the words they read through Pangram, a tool to detect AI writing, or other such detectors. Almost every writer I know has some visceral repulsion at the tells — “tapestry,” “crystallize,” “delve,” or “it’s not X, it’s Y” — that low-effort, overfitted register. Probably no one online reacts more violently than the British writer Sam Kriss, in an essay titled “If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you”:

I hate it. I find it viscerally disgusting; a cold shudder like someone’s poured jelly down the back of my neck. I hate that it’s everywhere; I hate that when I read basically anything now I’m constantly on alert, twitching like a schizo in an underpass. Is this thing really what it says it is? Is this person actually a robot in disguise? Nice little personal essay you’ve got there, lady, but I know what you really are; time to get my knife out, time to start digging around under your skin until I find the wires.

This urge — when a sentence feels off, and you must dig beneath its skin to find the wires — might be familiar to you. At a conference not long ago, I watched Chris Best, Substack’s chief executive, and Oliver Habryka, who runs the rationalist forum LessWrong, discuss this disturbance. Both platforms, in their early days, were built on the assumption that a reader can trust the writing in front of them to be authentic and human (and distinctive from institutional writing). Today, that assumption no longer holds.

LessWrong now requires its writers to disclose when they have used AI. As of publication, Substack has also recently launched a feature using Pangram-style detection to reduce “Claudefishing,” so readers don’t “unwittingly invest their attention in something with no human thought on the other end.” Everyone seems exhausted by the constant tax of suspecting AI behind every sentence. The tech industry’s actions and inaction (LinkedIn, for instance, has become a dumpster of AI slop people laugh at) reflect a growing backlash against soulless slop.

I, too, have struggled with anger over sloppy AI writing that has made me viscerally uncomfortable. My reactions can be a little pathological: I fanatically delete my own em dashes, and I once even mistakenly thought a few sentences a writer friend wrote were AI-generated. But I also must confess to my own relationship with AI: Because English is my second language, I rely heavily on Claude as a grammar checker— to smooth the bumps in my sentences and remove the ESL flavor. I used to have a somewhat cringy analogy to describe writing in English: installing a pair of mechanical wings. These wings carry me to vast terrains and audiences I couldn’t reach before, even though they sometimes feel artificial. AI makes those wings less heavy, but more not-entirely-me. So when I do get angry at AI writing, I also try to understand where the anger comes from — and then I wonder how angry I am allowed to be.

Escaping The Simplified Chinese Internet

For a long time, I felt trapped in my mother tongue after I left China at the age of 17. More precisely, I mean a particular kind of language born out of China’s enclosed internet. It is a strange language that sticks with you — long since severed from the depth and philosophical richness of Chinese — tamed and flattened by years of shrinking space for discussion and infested with algorithm-favored brevity.

Out of self-mockery and sympathy, people coined a term, the “Simplified Chinese Internet” (简中互联网). It is a phrase that immediately suggests crippled thoughts, one-dimensional topics, evasively coded slang that dodges censorship yet means nothing, alongside advanced infrastructure and intense scrutiny. It was the Simplified Chinese internet itself that I wanted to escape. And the language used on it can be understood as the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today’s LLM training. Over time, even the most creative and rebellious minds are tamed and overfitted, until they can only produce “acceptable” continuations — for public “safety.” Of course, precisely because the “Simplified Chinese Internet” is constrained and censored, it can sometimes inspire strange, ingenious ways of expressing discontent. The 2022 “White Paper” protests are a perfect example: Demonstrators opposed Zero-COVID by holding up blank sheets of paper, because the state (and the algorithms) can’t censor emptiness. But such cleverness is not a credit to censorship itself, or evidence that authoritarian control doesn’t suffocate creativity and self-expression. That conclusion would be utterly wrong. In reality, most of those who are “unsafe” simply left the “Simplified Chinese Internet” long ago or became idle.

That kind of creative poverty makes me think about LLMs’ inability to be original writers. In the past couple of months, many people using LLMs to write stories have noticed a strange effect: a disproportionate number of stories about lighthouses, clockmakers and librarians — and these stories would always feature a protagonist named “Elias Thorne.” Elias’s name now turns up everywhere: on self-published Amazon books, fake news sites and YouTube videos. It’s a typical phenomenon of model collapse — a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity outputs. One unverified guess is that alignment makes LLMs prefer the “safest” options during post-training, which steers them from saying things that are low-reward (inappropriate content, copyright infringement, etc.). An LLM will avoid every possible minefield and choose outputs that maximize the reward within its system parameters, so we’ll end up with a story about a lonely Elias Thorne living in a lighthouse at the edge of the world. It’s almost like asking an 18-year-old Chinese student to tell a story on a test: the result is a cookie-cutter lineup of Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — morality-driven, legible packages that reliably earn a good Gaokao score.

But we wicked human beings, especially in creative fields, are very good at working against all of the above. As writer Celine Nguyen said, “the core obligation of the artwork is to move me, not to make itself legible to me.” What great writing might never come to be in a reward-and-punishment regime solely intent on maximizing the score? I learned the answer to that, oddly enough, in childhood with the 19th-century French poet Baudelaire.

I am still amused and haunted by that accidental childhood encounter with his Gothic and sinful poems on death, hell, sex and decay in “Les Fleurs du mal,” or “The Flowers of Evil.”

I was probably 8 or 9, reaching up to the lower shelf of my father’s bookcase in our home in Taiyuan, in northern China, looking for something less childish to read. The cover had convinced me the book was about some Greek heroes and European adventures. It was a small, old book, brittle-paged, translated by scholar Guo Hong’an. My father, who I suspect never read Baudelaire closely himself, only told me the poet was a great man. “A Western master, like Shakespeare, Dickens, Victor Hugo. A classic!” He said it with reverence, and with the delight of a father whose daughter had reached for the West so young.

“Quote his lines in your homework essays next week,” my father suggested. And so, without warning, I walked into Baudelaire’s imagination before I knew what “Western master” meant, and the most intrusive, alienating passages imprinted themselves on me — in a Chinese translation that was both beautiful and terrifying.

My father — a trend-chasing magazine editor in northern China, longing for America and liberalism — had bought the book in his early 20s, during one of PRC’s rather open, pluralistic stretches, when the country allowed itself to discuss Baudelaire in daylight. Through the Cultural Revolution, when the only safe-to-read book was Mao’s “Little Red Book,” the literary establishment took its cue from Soviet doctrine and filed Baudelaire’s writings under the decadence of late, rotting capitalism; to read him was heresy, a “poison” of degeneracy.

And yet he survived, passed hand to hand in secret by underground readers in Beijing, Shanghai, even in the steep mountains of Chongqing. Bei Dao, an iconoclastic poet my father once admired, has written about what those smuggled poems meant in the dark times: We scavenged together for Baudelaire’s scattered poems, as if looking for a needle in the sea, and copied them down carefully and neatly into notebooks. For the Beijing underground literary world, such samizdat was a kind of spiritual guide.

Many years later, now living in California, I can still describe that childhood afternoon in China with “Les Fleurs du mal” as a terrifying, exciting, gut-wrenching ride. Those poems are about blood-sucking vampires and sexual desire and rotting corpses and a seductive woman decaying into a gruesome pile of bones by the roadside. They were nothing like the Chinese children’s books, nothing like my textbooks, nothing like any Western classic I’d been handed. I knew enough to understand I was reading something forbidden, something that had slipped through a crack and that my father would probably take it back the moment he realized what it was.

I never did take my father’s advice and quote Baudelaire in my homework. It took me a while to scrub the shock and the shame of reading him out of my head. His deeper hold surfaced only in adulthood, and only years later. Only once I had read more widely did I understand what he actually was. All that moral trespass, he had poured into the strictest inherited forms of French verse (the alexandrine, the quatrain, the sonnet). Inside those orderly meters the reader does not find the themes the form trains you to expect. Shock is the point. 

Baudelaire was prosecuted the instant “Les Fleurs du mal” appeared, in the summer of 1857 — charged by French authorities with both blasphemy and what the court called an outrage to public decency; he was convicted for indecency, and six of his poems were ordered removed from the book. Condemned in Paris; then, a century on, condemned again by Maoist orthodoxy as bourgeois rot. He resurfaced in the loosening China of the 1980s and ’90s and was collected by hungry liberal young men like my father, who mistook the most subversive 19th-century book in our house for Western canon.

Strangely, AI is what recently sent me back to Baudelaire. Against all that balanced, polished and polite prose written by machines using a mixture of statistical centrality and learning from human feedback scores, I found myself missing Baudelaire — missing the bookshelf, the second one down, which stayed faintly sinful for years. Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.

Good Taste?

My friend Jerry Zhou, who worked on LLM training at Microsoft AI, told me a model is like a single person, and millions of people around the world are all asking that one person questions. If the questions are similar, the answers converge. And unless you intervene at the level of the LLM weights or training objective, you should never expect this person to surprise you, and especially not shock you.

Claude’s own “Constitution,” a document some 80 pages long that teaches the model how to behave, instructs it to be “genuinely good, wise, and virtuous”: to be tactful, helpful, graceful, honest and, above all, to “help people in the way a good person would.” And I wonder whether today’s Baudelaire archetypes, those writers and artists out there, would ever want to create what a “good person” would create. To many, I suspect the phrase itself might insult their craft or be stultifying.

I keep returning to a line from Simon Schama’s “The Power of Art.” It is the book’s first sentence: “great art has dreadful manners.” Schama, a historian at Columbia University, tells us that art is a “thug,” “merciless and wily.” It will “grab you in a headlock, rough up your composure, and then proceed in short order to re-arrange your sense of reality.”

I admit it is unfair to expect every writer and artist to be as provocative as Baudelaire. But that episode from my childhood formed an early conviction: that greatness can arrive in the margins,  be deemed unsafe and still elude any empirical measure. That a “Western master” need not be a Dickens or a Hugo, one of those virtuous authors who “care for the proletariat and the downtrodden,” as PRC curriculum prefers. He can just as well be a man condemned, across more than a century, by the French courts and Maoism alike.

That afternoon, after I slid Baudelaire back onto the shelf, I went to my desk and finished my homework. In the years after, I must have written countless essays, all of them obedient to the specifications of the Chinese education system, perfectly legible to my teachers. Neither they nor I would remember a single one. Even now I am still trying to unlearn the muscle memory those schools and the Simplified Chinese internet drilled into me.

Posterity’s verdict on Baudelaire is that he is the last poet of French classicism and the first of French modernism. That evil book would, many years on, make him the father of French Symbolism. Nearly 100 years later, on May 31, 1949, the judgment against him was formally overturned, and the six banned poems were returned to print in France. The great 20th-century critic Walter Benjamin called him the forerunner of the modern poet, locked in a life-or-death struggle with the urban commodity capitalism then rising in an industrializing Paris — one that no one yet knew how to describe. In an old France without Baudelaire, no one had the language for the new urban reality that modernity had produced. Baudelaire, however, displayed what Benjamin described as the “shocking, raw immediacy of his sense impressions” of that reality, which is full of sensations of modernity like prostitutes, mud, gaslight, jostling crowds and perpetual alienation.

In a mercantile Paris, who needed what Benjamin called “a ragpicker who gathers up the city’s detritus only to turn it into poetry”? Who could have imagined that this ragpicker would become a representative figure of modernity’s decay? The blind spot the researcher Zhengdong Wang names in judging what an LLM can do, in an essay on AI evaluation, is a blind spot in human society too: “We don’t even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change.” Yes, the world didn’t know it wanted a Baudelaire, for a long time, until it understood him. The old coordinates, like the French state that prosecuted Baudelaire and took his 50 francs, can neither permit nor comprehend an experience that is invisible and wholly real. This, I think, is the very sensation my father’s generation went looking for, those Chinese who came of age in the Cultural Revolution. Baudelaire had leaped clear of every measure his society used to sort “good” from “bad”, and was punished for the leap. Bei Dao, the poet who kept Baudelaire as a secret spiritual icon through those years, went on with his peers, in the more open China of the 1980s, to found the Misty Poetry movement that deeply influenced my father. The movement was set against almost everything the Cultural Revolution’s benchmarks had prized—those socialist-realist works and political lyric poems marked by positive emotion, educational value, with the author cast as a representative of “the people” or “the era”—and instead was filled with the unknowable and the unforeseen.

Today’s Silicon Valley somewhat resembles the French state that punished Baudelaire, an age intoxicated by abundance and by its own industrial revolution. We are being persuaded that AI will hand us prosperity and an intelligence explosion, that it will cure cancer any day now. The researchers working on recursive self-improvement have convinced me that AI will excel at every benchmark we can put into words. And yet the awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.

AI feels disenchanted; it didn’t “revolutionize” content. It’s increasingly “same-ifying” writing, design, and everything related to human expression, and shaping our thoughts in reverse. Over the last few years, many in Silicon Valley have held up “taste” as an antidote. People argue that “good taste” makes one’s eye discerning and can identify ineffable qualities that stand out in the ocean of infinite content generated by AI. For leaders, “taste is a competitive advantage,” an article in The Atlantic claims. Culture critic and software designer Celine Nguyen observed that “taste has become the catch-all term,” and Kyle Chayka, a staff writer at The New Yorker, suggested it has become the latest Silicon Valley cliché — like “disruption” was in the 2010s. The word has hardened into something widely repeated and inherently profitable, a lever for correcting what AI produces. Taste is the new moat, these AI entrepreneurs say.

The term has also traveled to China and its equally pervasive AI industry. On the Simplified Chinese internet, the tech junkies and AI practitioners trade notes on how to build things with “good taste.” My internal seismograph reads otherwise. Some of this “good taste” will soon become the new mid-curve of mediocrity, the new predictability, the new “it’s not X, it’s Y.” Baudelaire would have no use for it. He was a man who deliberately set out to provoke revulsion. He believed “the mixture of the grotesque and the tragic is as pleasing to the mind as dissonances to blasé ears.” A man proud of his bad taste. “What is exhilarating in bad taste,” he wrote in his private journals, “is the aristocratic pleasure of giving offense.”

articles.title: Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences
articles.summary: When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue…
articles.content:
When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

At Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

1. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play

It’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something new. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty

2. Small moments can lead to meaningful choices

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible. 

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.  

In our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. 
 
Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.  

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.  

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part. 

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.  

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur

3. Connecting with someone across a difference isn’t about erasing what separates us

 
I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences. 

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones

4. Disagreement can actually bring us closer together and create new opportunities

In my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang

5. Character development is often uncomfortable, but the payoff is worth it

Working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III

6. Intellectual humility and curiosity pair well together; when in doubt, admit what you don’t know and let your curiosity guide you forward

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It shows that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

articles.title: Only Genuine Compassion Will Do
articles.summary: It's not enough to simply to believe compassion is important. We must transform our thoughts and behavior on a daily basis to cultivate compassion. The post Only Genuine Compassion Will Do appeared first on Lion’s Roar.
articles.content:
Before we can generate compassion and love, it is important to have a clear understanding of what we understand compassion and love to be. In simple terms, compassion and love can be defined as positive thoughts and feelings that give rise to such essential things in life as hope, courage, determination, and inner strength. In the Buddhist tradition, compassion and love are seen as two aspects of the same thing: Compassion is the wish for another being to be free from suffering; love is wanting them to have happiness.

It is not enough to believe that compassion is important and to think about how nice it is!

Self-centeredness inhibits our love for others, and we are all afflicted by it to one degree or another. For true happiness to come about, we need a calm mind, and such peace of mind is brought about only by a compassionate attitude. How can we develop this attitude? Obviously, it is not enough for us simply to believe that compassion is important and to think about how nice it is! We need to make a concerted effort to develop it; we must use all the events of our daily life to transform our thoughts and behavior.

Many forms of compassionate feeling are mixed with desire and attachment. For instance, the love parents feel for their child is often strongly associated with their own emotional needs, so it is not fully compassionate. Usually when we are concerned about a close friend, we call this compassion, but it too is usually attachment. Even in marriage, the love between husband and wife—particularly at the beginning, when each partner still may not know the other’s deeper character very well—depends more on attachment than genuine love. Marriages that last only a short time do so because they lack compassion; they are produced by emotional attachment based on projection and expectation, and as soon as the projections change, the attachment disappears. Our desire can be so strong that the person to whom we are attached appears flawless, when in fact he or she has many faults. In addition, attachment makes us exaggerate small, positive qualities. When this happens, it indicates that our love is motivated more by personal need than by genuine care for another.

Compassion without attachment is possible. Therefore, we need to clarify the distinctions between compassion and attachment. True compassion is not just an emotional response but a firm commitment founded on reason. Because of this firm foundation, a truly compassionate attitude toward others does not change even if they behave negatively. Genuine compassion is based not on our own projections and expectations, but rather on the needs of the other: irrespective of whether another person is a close friend or an enemy, as long as that person wishes for peace and happiness and wishes to overcome suffering, then on that basis we develop genuine concern for their problem. This is genuine compassion. For a Buddhist practitioner, the goal is to develop this genuine compassion, this genuine wish for the well-being of another, in fact for every living being throughout the universe.

Adapted from The Compassionate Life, by the Dalai Lama. © 2001 Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama. Available from Wisdom Publications.

articles.title: DD402 / Agency, not abstinence
articles.summary: Issue 402: Agency, not abstinence – Read the full issue in the archive.
articles.content:
When in the mid 2010s the first Silicon Valley folks started warning us about the addictive nature of social media, the idea that it wasn’t really our fault felt like a relief. We were being manipulated by algorithms designed to keep us scrolling, our brains rewired by dopamine hits, our attention harvested.

A decade later, that diagnosis still holds true, but we also turned a complicated problem into a very convenient story: we are simply the helpless victims of deceptive design and exploitative algorithms.

Kate Wagner doesn’t buy into the victim story. In her recent essay, she criticises the increasingly elaborate genre of phone-detox evangelism – the books, apps, browser extensions, courses and dumb phones to help us ‘reclaim our lives’. She’s sceptical of the commercialisation of it, and even more sceptical of the promise behind it – that putting down your phone will somehow transform you into a more creative and fulfilled person.

Rather than treating phone use as an addiction we need to defeat, she suggests we should ask what we’re actually getting from it:

“In order to quit, one must realize that what is really being interrogated is not necessarily the thing itself (and yes this includes Phone Capitalism) but the behavior and what we get out of it. What do we want from Phone World? Is it companionship? Prestige? Reassurance seeking? Attention? Entertainment? What do we get from doomscrolling? Why even call it that? Can we not use grown-up words like self-soothing, numbing, rumination, avoidance, paranoia, insecurity, anxiety, despondency, resentment, despair, anger etc. to describe our behaviors and the feelings behind them?”

“Ultimately, phone use is not an existential battle between the human mind and nefarious powerless-making material and mechanical forces – it is a behavior.”

Shaming yourself for having no willpower doesn’t do much, and neither does waging war on your dopamine receptors. What works better is noticing what you’re feeling, creating a little distance between the impulse and the action, and finding another way of responding to it.

Wagner draws on techniques from Dialectical Behaviour Therapy for this – small, sometimes almost comically simple interventions that interrupt an impulse without requiring you to somehow become a more disciplined or enlightened person.

Even if you manage to log off, she argues, you probably won’t read the complete works of Dostoyevsky, overthrow capitalism and discover your ‘authentic self’ with all that newfound free time. You might just be bored and eventually find other – hopefully healthier – ways to channel whatever it was you were looking for on your phone.

To be clear, I’m not defending Big Tech here, and neither is she. There are many good reasons to worry about what our phones and the platforms are doing to our attention, our social lives and our ability to be bored without immediately reaching for stimulation.

But I appreciate Wagner’s counterpoint to the increasingly melodramatic detox narrative: we do have more agency than we’ve been led to believe, and getting more of our lives back doesn’t need to involve becoming a different person or buying an ever-growing collection of crutches.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

articles.title: Home is where the land is
articles.summary: Piece by piece, the land was stolen. As Wilson Williams — a band council member of the Indigenous Squamish Nation in British Columbia, Canada — tells it, the creeping land grab by non-Indigenous settlers reached official status in 1877, whe…
articles.content:
Piece by piece, the land was stolen. As Wilson Williams — a band council member of the Indigenous Squamish Nation in British Columbia, Canada — tells it, the creeping land grab by non-Indigenous settlers reached official status in 1877, when Canada’s federal government confined his ancestors to living on a 34-hectare reserve. Up until that time, they had flourished in and around the ancient village of Sen̓áḵw, a seaside trading hub at the mouth of False Creek in what is today Vancouver.

“Sen̓áḵw was a place of abundance,” Williams says. “People hunted elk, beaver, duck and deer; they fished for salmon. And they had access to lumber,” he explains, referring to the cedars used to build longhouses and make dug-out canoes. But the colonizers even started taking chunks of the reserve land (making meaningless the definition of “reserve”) to make way for railroad extensions and industrial expansion, all of which accelerated after the Great Fire of Vancouver in 1886. The final death knell to what remained of Sen̓áḵw came in 1913, when the provincial government of British Columbia evicted the Squamish people from the reserve and burned down their homes. “Police gave them two days’ notice to leave,” says Williams, his great-grandfather being one of the dispossessed. “Those who refused to leave because they didn’t want to lose the connection to their land were loaded onto a barge and set adrift.” 

For Indigenous people, for whom connection to land means connection to self, expulsion from one’s ancestral territory is tantamount to being made homeless — “home” signifying much more than the dwellings, be they temporary or permanent, erected on that land. In Indigenous ontologies, home is also the land that supports those structures and feeds the life and community, the stories and ceremonies that take shape in and around them. This contrasts with the Western notion of home, which tends to mean “housing,” limiting the potential for wellbeing to the shelter offered by a house and the value wrested from it when treated as a commodity.

The fate forced upon the Squamish people — the twin dispossession of land and destruction of homes — is a history repeated in many parts of the world.

In the countries that are today referred to as Canada, Australia and New Zealand, as British colonizers evicted Indigenous peoples from their lands, they also placed a chokehold on Indigenous self-determination. They outlawed governance systems and ceremonies that had thrived for millennia and snuffed out economies, knowledges and livelihoods grounded in communal wellbeing and kinship with the land. In so doing, they also erased the physical spaces and dwellings people inhabited, from First Nations longhouses and Māori marae and papakāinga to the multitudes of housing typologies designed by the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island peoples in so-called Australia to respond to differences in climate, culture and material availability.

While home and housing are not necessarily the same, one can determine or influence the other, with consequences for health outcomes. When people are robbed of the title to or ownership of their land, they no longer control what happens on it, including policies to do with the construction of and access to housing. As the Crown in Australia, New Zealand and Canada deported Indigenous peoples from their lands of plenty into poverty on government-determined reserves, it forced them into shoddily built and culturally inappropriate houses meant merely to provide a roof but not to nourish community, good health and wellbeing. The colonial policies created housing insecurity, overcrowding and homelessness.

These impacts of colonialism on Indigenous housing reverberates today. According to Canada’s 2021 census, people in First Nations communities are four times more likely to live in crowded conditions and six times more likely to live in houses in poor repair than non-Indigenous people; the Inuit are 40 percent more likely than the non-Indigenous population to be housing insecure. In Australia, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, in a report under the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Performance Framework, shows similar statistics for Indigenous housing, with First Nations people facing discrimination in accessing quality housing and being less likely than non-Indigenous Australians to have the financial means to buy or rent secure homes in good repair. What’s more, the rate of First Nations people being unhoused is almost 10 times higher than for the non-Indigenous population. The Indigenous housing crises in Canada and Australia are mirrored in Aotearoa New Zealand, where Māori are five times more likely than non-Indigenous people to be unhoused and where the homeownership rate for Māori is only 28 percent compared with 57 percent for non-Māori, per the government’s 2023 report “An evaluation of whānau experiences of living in contracted emergency housing.”

Today, however, Indigenous peoples in Canada, Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand are rewriting that narrative by increasingly taking control of what housing can and should look like and building quality homes that fit their specific needs at affordable prices. And increasingly, this happens on land returned to Indigenous peoples as part of land claims, as in Canada, or as part of the Crown making amends for having broken treaties it signed with Indigenous nations, as with the breaches to Te Tiriti o Waitangi in Aotearoa New Zealand. Take the Tauhara North No. 2 Trust, based in Rotorua on the north end of Te Ika-a-Māui, or the North Island. The trust has as its core goals to provide services within the scopes of health and education for its iwi, or tribe. “But you can’t have health if you don’t have quality housing,” says Wikitoria Hepi-Te Huia. So the trust also runs a housing division, Tauhara North Kaitiaki Whenua, of which Hepi-Te Huia is the director. The housing arm is in the process of building homes for its iwi, an endeavour that reflects the broader spirit of the National Māori Housing Strategy, a Māori-Crown partnership that aims to uphold the right to secure, quality housing as a cornerstone of building a better future for all Māori.

A key motto and cultural aspect of the Māori is Toitū te whenua (Hold fast to the land), reflecting the Indigenous idea of home as being more than just the dwelling one occupies. When the British colonizers stole the land — the whenua — of the Māori, they inflicted on them a similarly violent uprooting as that suffered by the Squamish people in British Columbia. The Māori, like their brethren across the Pacific Ocean, were set adrift in a system foreign to them and deaf to their ways of living. And so, for Hepi-Te Huia, access to housing is a social justice issue that needs to be addressed in a holistic way. “For us,” she says, referring to the trust and to her iwi, “it’s not about housing; it’s about building homes.” At the trust’s brand-new Hamlin Road development in Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland — a 30-home complex inaugurated on April 6 with much optimism for the future — families have now moved into bright apartments of varying sizes to suit their needs. “People need quality homes where they can feel safe and secure, not at risk of having to move again and again,” says Hepi-Te Huia, reflecting a common occurrence for many marginalized Māori living in substandard government-run social housing.

“Our goal is to build homes for the long term, where people can live for many years, even their whole lives.”

The model, and the Hamlin Road homes, was realized with grant funding from the Crown and income from an energy partnership the trust has in a geothermal project. It offers subsidized housing, at 80 percent of market rent, but residents able to pay market rent can do so and funnel the 20 percent on top of the subsidized rent into savings they can use to eventually purchase their homes. The long-term thinking opens avenues for flexibility that wouldn’t be possible without the trust exercising control over the housing it’s providing.

For the Squamish people, it was long-term thinking that would put them at the vanguard of housing innovation in Canada. After decades of legal wrangling to take back their land — work that was partly spearheaded by Williams’s great-grandfather, Andy Paull — the Squamish Nation in 2002 won a British Columbia court decision that ordered the railway company to give back a 4.2-hectare parcel in downtown Vancouver, where the village of Sen̓áḵw had once been located. That sliver of ancestral land is now being converted into a mega housing project, or, as Williams puts it, “the largest Indigenous land development in Canadian history.” Named Sen̓áḵw and carried out through a 50-50 partnership with Vancouver-based real-estate developer West Bank, the project will feature 6,000-plus rental apartments, including 1,200 affordable units and 250 “deeply affordable” apartments for Squamish Nation members. “It’s reconciliation in action,” says Wilson, adding that the high-rises will add sorely needed rentals for the general population in a city that suffers from a chronic housing shortage. But the rentals model is foremost a deliberate strategy to ensure long-term income. “Sen̓áḵw represents sustainable economic development for our people and future generations,” Wilson says.

Designed to be environmentally sustainable, it will be the largest net-zero community in Canada, showing the world how the Squamish people are stewards of their homeland.

While the Squamish Nation has been able to negotiate a modern land claim that has given it the autonomy to scale up its housing model, and the Tauhara North No. 2 Trust has been able to build homes for its iwi on Māori land, the concept of “land back” is not something that Indigenous people in Australia can take for granted. In fact, the government of Australia, and the British Crown before it, has never entered into a treaty with First Nations people that gives them land rights. As a result, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people have little to no control over land, making it difficult to implement a social-justice framework for Indigenous housing. As Kieran Wong — co-founder and partner at the Fulcrum Agency, a Fremantle-based (and non-Indigenous) architecture firm that works almost exclusively with First Nations in rural and remote areas — says, this lack of land rights needs to be completely overhauled. “My home is on land I own, that I have title to. It’s called green title, and with it I can do whatever I want or say no to whatever I don’t want on my land, like a cattle ranch. But Native title in Australia only gives Indigenous people the right to be there, but not to make decisions as to what happens on the land,” Wong explains. So if a mining company wants to start exploiting Indigenous land, the First Nation that has lived there for millennia has no legal right to oppose it as they don’t have title.

Add to the land rights injustice the colonial-inflicted intersection of trauma and poverty and a paternalistic housing policy, and you’ve got a system that has ostensibly tried to “help” by offering funding for housing, and then repeatedly defunding and killing those programs. “A major challenge with funding for Indigenous housing initiatives in Australia is that governments fund bedrooms to deal with overcrowding as opposed to funding housing as a whole,” Wong says.

“But for First Nations people, overcrowding is not what drives the conversation; what matters to them is maintaining kinship ties, movement between communities, mobility.”

Here, as in Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland and Vancouver, the Indigenous notion of home goes far beyond the narrow, Western concept of housing. “People tend to think about houses, but the bigger issues are land, infrastructure, affordability and durability,” Wong says.

On a more micro level, but with major importance for the First Nations looking to improve housing for their members, Wong says that while he can’t change building codes or housing policies, his firm can — and is — working with Indigenous communities to create culturally appropriate homes that are built to last. This starts even before entering a client relationship. “We don’t go after First Nations clients, because it’s not up to us to determine their needs or dictate what they should want. We only enter a client relationship after the client has come to us. And that’s when our job is to listen and learn,” says Wong. This puts the First Nation in the driver’s seat from the outset, whether the client is looking for Fulcrum to design homes, provide support on funding and grant applications or envision infrastructure upgrades. Despite the numerous roadblocks slowing down progress in First Nations housing in Australia, several communities have successfully implemented housing initiatives that serve their needs — including the Anindilyakwa Housing Aboriginal Corporation on Groote Eylandt, an island off the northeast coast of Northern Territory, which represents the first time an Indigenous community in Australia decided how it wanted its homes to be built.

As examples in Canada, Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand show, when Indigenous peoples are enabled to control their economic, social, political and cultural futures — and when architects listen to their needs when it comes to designing housing — they create socially and culturally sensitive homes that respond to the needs of their communities and sometimes even of the broader society. Indigenous housing must be controlled by Indigenous people to address the injustices and inequities that linger from colonial-imposed marginalization. But for full control of housing, Indigenous people need to gain control of their homelands. In the meantime, they are rebuilding their cultures, their economies, their homes. Brick by brick, log by log, they are constructing their own destinies. Only then can they be secure in the knowledge that they will not be set adrift into the unknown.

Traditional groundbreaking celebrations at the future site of Sen̓áḵw: a 6,000-plus rental housing precinct on Squamish lands, for Squamish Nations members. Video: Sen̓áḵw

The post Home is where the land is first appeared on Assemble Papers.

articles.title: How To Find And Keep Joy
articles.summary: Today it’s all about passion. Find your passion. Live passionately. Inspire the world with your passion. Passion, we tell ourselves, is the source of joy. The Stoics disagreed. In fact, they believed that passion(s) were what contributed to…
articles.content:
Today it’s all about passion. Find your passion. Live passionately. Inspire the world with your passion. Passion, we tell ourselves, is the source of joy.

The Stoics disagreed. In fact, they believed that passion(s) were what contributed to our misery. To the experts and gurus who assure us that passion—that unbridled enthusiasm, that willingness to pounce on what’s in front of us with the full measure of our zeal—is our most important asset, Seneca would ask, “how can such wavering and unstable persons possess any good that is fixed and lasting?

So what should we pursue? Where do we find joy? And how do we keep it? Seneca’s answer comes in his letter, On the True Joy which Comes from Philosophy:

“It comes from a good conscience, from honorable purposes, from right actions, from contempt of the gifts of chance, from an even and calm way of living which treads but one path…There are only a few who control themselves and their affairs by a guiding purpose; the rest do not proceed; they are merely swept along, like objects afloat in a river. And of these objects, some are held back by sluggish waters and are transported gently; others are torn along by a more violent current; some, which are nearest the bank, are left there as the current slackens; and others are carried out to sea by the onrush of the stream. Therefore, we should decide what we wish, and abide by the decision.”

Unshakeable joy comes from purpose. In something bigger than yourself. In perspective and gratitude. In the wisdom that philosophy teaches us. It might not be as exciting or as glamorous. It might be a little slower. But it’s far more durable and meaningful.

Finding that will take time and work and self-reflection. But it’s in there. Inside you. Dig deep. Find it. And you’ll have joy you can hold onto forever.

The post How To Find And Keep Joy appeared first on Daily Stoic.

articles.title: The Typographic Details Behind Typewolf’s Favorite Sites of September 2018
articles.summary: This is the 56th installment of my monthly feature on Typewolf where I share my favorite type-driven websites from the previous month and then write a little about the typographic details behind the designs. You can check out last month’s p…
articles.content:
This is the 56th installment of my monthly feature on Typewolf where I share my favorite type-driven websites from the previous month and then write a little about the typographic details behind the designs. You can check out last month’s post for August here.

Leader Bag Co

Ogg is a beautiful serif that is full of character and personality. It has some unusual features, such as the lower stroke on the e that tends to stick out into the letter that follows it, but that is what makes it so unique and memorable. It’s combined here with Freight Text for body copy and Pitch Sans for navigation and captions. I love the colorful, childlike illustrations, but they feel a little out of place next to the products being sold which come across as more chic and fashionable than fun and quirky.

Notation

This is the first use of Halyard I’ve featured on Typewolf which is a little surprising as the entire family is readily available on Adobe Fonts (Typekit), and Joshua Darden’s other superfamily, Freight, has been massively popular for quite a long time. The design of Halyard was influenced by the classic grotesques of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, but it feels a little more even and regular compared to the grotesques of that era which often feel a little off-kilter and wonky. It’s paired here with Freight Display which is used at large sizes for headlines (as intended), while Freight Text is used for body copy. The Freight and Halyard families pair together nicely, as is oftentimes the case with typefaces from the same designer.

The Story of Vermont’s Quiet Digital Revolution

I love the Q on Colophon’s Mabry typeface—it was the perfect choice for setting the title here as it immediately stands out and gives a distinctive look to the branding. It contrasts nicely with the serif Larish Neue, set directly above it. The body text, set in Graphik, has a readable, narrow width, and the pullquotes breaking out from the grid make the page feel more dynamic. The wide-bodied Adieu is used for bylines and labels, and a fourth sans-serif, Helvetica, is used sporadically as well but probably isn’t really needed since there are already three other sans-serifs being used.

Porter & Pals

When I first saw this site, I had no idea it was for a dog food company as the branding is completely bizarre. But I think it is brilliant. As a dog owner myself, I know that the market for specialty dog food is completely saturated—and every brand kind of looks the same. Porter & Pals are probably aware of this and wanted to do something to quickly distinguish themselves from their sea of competitors. And I think they have succeeded here. Their brand feels crazy and exciting and different from anything else out there.

The type plays a huge role in this. The sans-serif Danzza is a geometric/grotesque hybrid that feels genuinely happy—the oversized tail on the g makes it look like it is smiling at you. Windsor has a retro charm that exudes warmth. And Suisse Int’l Mono has a techie feel that matches the aesthetic of the colorful gradients. The type choices, combined with the imagery and colors, come together to create one of the most memorable brands I’ve seen.

articles.title: 'Captain EO' at 40: Michael Jackson's wild sci-fi movie that you could only watch at Disney theme parks
articles.summary: Remember when the King of Pop joined forces with Coppola, Lucas and Disney for an inspiring 3D space musical?
articles.content:
40 years ago on Sept. 12, 1986, musical icon Michael Jackson debuted in "Captain EO," a 17-minute long 3D sci-fi fantasy film. The catch? You could only see it at Walt Disney World's EPCOT Center in Florida, or — six days later — at Disneyland’s Magic Eye Theater over in Tomorrowland.

Jackson had already been anointed the King of Pop in the ‘80s with the stellar multi-platinum album "Thriller" when the creative cosmic tumblers aligned, joining the immense talents of Jackson, George Lucas, Francis Ford Coppola and the wizards of Disney's Imagineering to create one of the most unique sci-fi entertainment offerings ever conceived.

With impressive special effects, catchy songs, dynamic dance numbers and co-starring Academy Award-winning actress Anjelica Huston as the witch queen known as the Supreme Leader, "Captain EO" was a huge attraction seen by millions of Disney guests.

It told the story of a rag-tag crew of space misfits led by Jackson's charismatic Captain EO (in a sweet white leather uniform) on a mission to a sinister industrial planet to deliver a mysterious gift to its despotic ruler. Plenty of hijinks ensue with EO's oddball companions: Major Domo, Hooter, Idy & Ody, and a winged kitten creature named Fuzzball.

After crash landing on the dark world directly onto the homing beacon, EO and his crazy crew are apprehended by a gang of warrior henchmen and hauled into the throne room to face the wicked alien ruler who is imprisoned in anger and hate.

Huston is electrifying in her Giger-esque makeup, supported by a tangle of banded black cables and sporting long fingernails that were deliciously thrust into audiences’ eyes using the magic of 3D and the special red-and-blue-lensed glasses handed out when arriving for each screening.

When EO's crew manifests into a musical band to offer a song to the Supreme Leader, Hooter trips over the power cord to ruin the performance. The commotion tries the queen’s patience and she dispatches her cruel Whip Warriors to capture EO and send him to her deepest, darkest dungeon.

But EO fights back with an illuminating t-shirt (hey, it was the '80s!), some fancy dance moves and a surge of musical energy to unlock her beauty. This transforms Huston into a colorful enchantress with her grim lair now becoming a lush Greek-like temple. Darkness turns to light and everyone leaves as peaceful galactic friends.

It's an honest plot with heart and humor filled with cool tunes and a sprinkling of in-your-face 3D moments for the whole family, and really, what else would you expect from a Jackson/Disney collaboration in the decade of excess?

The two prominent songs — the original "We Are Here to the Change the World," and "Another Part of Me" — are used to great effect throughout the simple narrative. I can fondly remember leaving the Magic Eye Theater the first time I saw it in the 1990s with an uplifted attitude and the renewed vigor needed to brave the epic summertime Disneyland crowds. Over the years I’d revisited the film a dozen times and it's remained a fun time capsule of unbridled spirit perfect for its age and even more relevant today.

Production began on "Captain EO" in the summer of 1985 with "Star Wars"' creator George Lucas serving as producer and legendary Francis Ford Coppola of The Godfather fame in the director's chair. James Horner, who’d later go on to compose the music for "Titanic," was enlisted to pen the original score. Essentially an expanded music video similar in format to 1983’s horror short, "Thriller," "Captain EO" was filmed entirely in Los Angeles with Lucas's ILM unit called in for a VFX polish.

Costing nearly $30 million to produce, "Captain EO" was, at the time, the most expensive short ever filmed on a per-minute basis. It was also a pioneering attraction that used in-theater 4D techniques that delivered floodlights, fog, smoke, starfields, meteors and LED laser effects out into the audience in conjunction with the added visual component of its 70MM 3D filming process.

"For all those who share Walt Disney's dream and delight in the promise of the future, we cut this ribbon signifying the opening of the 3-D musical motion picture space adventure, 'Captain EO!,'" proclaimed Coppola at its 1986 Disneyland premiere.

The attraction ran continuously at Disney World’s EPCOT Center until 1994 and lasted three years longer at Disneyland's Magic Kingdom before it was closed in 1997.

Upon Jackson’s untimely death in 2009 it returned for an encore tribute run between 2010 and 2015, including re-releases at Tokyo Disneyland and Disneyland Paris before vanishing completely to be locked up forever in the Disney Vault. It was also broadcast once though on MTV for a 1995 Michael Jackson tribute.

While an official Disney streaming option is nowhere to be found, there are YouTube channels that have uploaded enhanced and/or upscaled copies of "Captain EO" if you've got a hankering for some heart-warming sci-fi.

With so many dire warnings, dystopian fare and AI doomsdays prophesied everywhere you turn, maybe we all need a little bit of Captain EO's hopeful “The planets are linin' up, we're bringin' brighter days” message.

articles.title: CATL launches 170 Wh/kg battery platform for heavy-duty transport with 621-mile range
articles.summary: Diesel long dictated the roads, but electric heavy transport is taking charge. CATL unveiled its...
articles.content:
Diesel long dictated the roads, but electric heavy transport is taking charge. CATL unveiled its next-generation modular commercial vehicle battery platform, TECTRANS II, at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover. 

Rather than a basic cell update, the system is a adaptable modular architecture that integrates into existing vehicle lines. Truck manufacturers can achieve up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) of range on a single charge, backed by megawatt-level fast charging that replenishes 80% capacity in 25 minutes.

CATL rates the heavy-duty truck setup for a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer operating lifecycle while retaining 70 percent capacity.

“Commercial vehicle electrification is emerging as the third wave of the global energy transition,” said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. “Across products, energy, services and ecosystem, CATL is poised to work with partners around the world to catch this third wave.”

12 years of fleet duty

Diesel engines offered endless range, rapid refueling, and standard parts that kept maintenance cheap. On the other hand, battery electric alternatives meant heavy, expensive packs that ate into cargo limits and spent hours anchored to slow chargers.

That might finally be solved, thanks to CATL. TECTRANS II aims to simplify heavy vehicle electrification across diverse fleet operations. Its flexible modular design accommodates up to 1,000 kilometers of range and adapts easily to both charging and battery swapping. Manufacturers can standardize their chassis designs while upgrading battery chemistry over time.

Notably, standardized components will help developers to cut vehicle design timelines in half and slash early development costs. As a result, commercial fleets lower upfront investments and maximize operational returns throughout the vehicle lifecycle.

TECTRANS II boosts commercial vehicle profitability through lower upfront costs and higher daily operating returns. The battery delivers a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, exceeding the industry average by 13% and increasing payload capacity by 0.6 tonnes. 

Maximum configurations support megawatt fast charging to hit 80 percent capacity in 25 minutes. Interestingly, a full-tab low-impedance design drives system round-trip efficiency up to 96 percent to limit energy waste.

Ultra-durable TECTRANS II

Durability, however, is where CATL hopes to truly bury diesel. Fleet managers don’t care about sleek aesthetics, but more about uptime and resale value.

To prove the battery can handle harsh things, CATL designed a hot-formed steel cover capable of taking 10,000 steps from an 180-kilogram adult without deforming, paired with an armored bottom plate that withstands 1,000 Joules of road-debris impact. 

Inside it, independent multi-branch management systems mean that if a single battery line suffers a fault, it isolates automatically. And the rest of the pack continues delivering power, avoiding tow trucks and stranded cargo.

It also comes with standard 15-year corrosion resistance that protects units against harsh coastal and winter road conditions. 

CATL signed a Memorandum of Understanding with DHL Group to establish Green Freight Corridors across Europe, building on their prior late-2024 partnership. Combining DHL’s extensive logistics network with CATL’s battery technology, the companies will collaborate with vehicle manufacturers to design purpose-built electric trucks and launch pilot deployments along key transit routes.

“Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade,” said Zhu Lingbo, CTO of CATL Global Business Unit. 

With megawatt charging, standard modularity, and heavy haulage range finally in place, that decade-long shift looks less like a distant goal and more like an active rollout.
