articles.title: Elephant-skin tiles could help buildings stay cool without air conditioning
articles.summary: Researchers created elephant-inspired cement tiles that trap water and cool buildings through slow evaporation. The post Elephant-skin tiles could help buildings stay cool without air conditioning appeared first on The Brighter Side of News…
articles.content:
• Researchers have developed elephant-skin-inspired cement tiles that use microscopic pores and deliberately engineered cracks to capture, redistribute and slowly evaporate water for passive cooling.
  • In building-scale tests, temperatures beneath the new tiles remained around 89.6°F, compared with 107.6°F beneath cracked commercial stucco and 125.6°F beneath non-cracked stucco.
  • The design turns cracking, normally considered a structural defect, into a water-management system that could eventually help roofs and façades stay cooler while reducing demand for mechanical air conditioning.

Summer heat is becoming harder for buildings to handle. Air conditioning can protect people indoors, but it also uses large amounts of energy and pushes waste heat outside. A new study suggests part of the answer may come from an animal that cannot sweat.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and Syracuse University created cement-based tiles inspired by elephant skin. The tiles use planned cracks and tiny pores to trap water, spread it across a surface and cool buildings through slow evaporation.

The work shows how a simple material could cool roofs and façades without fans, compressors or moving parts. The design turns cracks, usually a sign of damage, into useful channels for water.

Learning From Elephant Skin

On hot days, people cool themselves through sweat. As moisture evaporates from skin, it pulls heat away. The process feels ordinary, but it is highly efficient.

Elephants face a tougher problem. They live under intense sun with thick, dark gray skin, yet they do not sweat like people do.

“Wrinkles,” said Dorit Aviv, an associate professor of architecture in the Weitzman School of Design. “Elephants have a network of cracks in their skin that trap water. When they spray themselves, that water stays put and evaporates slowly, cooling them over time.”

That idea came to Aviv through longtime collaborator Shu Yang, a materials scientist at Penn Engineering. It fit Aviv’s work on making buildings more thermally efficient.

The connection was direct. Buildings do not sweat either.

Why Buildings Need Passive Cooling

In the United States, people spend about 90% of their time indoors. Buildings also use about 40% of primary energy.

Nearly half of that building energy goes to heating, cooling and ventilation. As cities grow hotter, that demand is likely to rise.

“In the United States, we spend roughly 90% of our time indoors, and buildings consume about 40% of primary energy, nearly half of that for heating, cooling, and ventilation,” said Yang. “A passive, bio-inspired cooling façade like this could lower surface temperatures by 10-20° Fahrenheit compared to traditional stucco.”

Mechanical cooling can save lives during heat waves. But it also consumes electricity and dumps indoor heat outdoors.

A passive system works differently. It cools the building’s outer skin before heat moves inside.

Turning Cracks Into Canals

Evaporative cooling sounds simple. Add water, let it evaporate and remove heat.

But most building surfaces handle water poorly. Droplets bead up, bounce off or run down before they can cool much.

The research team needed a surface that could catch each droplet, hold it and move it with purpose. That led them back to cracks.

“In conventional construction, cracks signal weakness, the beginning of a material’s decline,” Yang said. “But by engineering where and how they form, we made networks of tiny channels that act like capillaries capable of pulling water across the surface and holding it in place.”

The team used ordinary Portland cement mixed with diatomaceous earth. This porous material comes from fossilized algae.

Together, they formed thin tiles that can store and transport water.

A Material With Two Jobs

The key insight was that water storage and water movement need different structures. The material had to do both well.

“We realized that storing water and moving water are actually two different problems,” said Kun-Hao Yu of Syracuse University. Yu conducted the experiments as a postdoctoral researcher in Yang’s lab.

“The microscopic pores inside the material act like tiny reservoirs that quickly soak up each droplet, while the engineered crack network acts like a system of canals that redistributes that water across the surface. It’s really the combination of those two features that lets the tile hold onto water instead of losing it.”

The pores absorb water in milliseconds. The cracks then move that water across the tile, even on sloped surfaces.

This keeps the surface wet longer. More time for evaporation means more cooling.

Making Cracks On Purpose

The tiles begin with a mixture of cement and diatomaceous earth. Researchers cast the material into thin shapes and let it partially hydrate.

They then dry it under carefully controlled conditions. As the material shrinks, stress builds inside it.

Instead of allowing random fractures, the team guides the stress along designed patterns. The result is a predictable lattice of cracks.

The researchers tested several crack patterns, including triangular, square and hexagonal designs. The hexagonal pattern performed especially well.

Its geometry forced water to move sideways in a zigzag path. That delayed drainage and kept more water on the surface.

Fast Water Capture, Slow Cooling

When water hits the tile, it does not bounce away. It quickly enters the pores and crack network.

In tests, the material absorbed droplets in less than 50 milliseconds. That fast capture helps prevent wasted water.

The crack network then spreads water laterally. On tilted tiles, the hexagonal layout helped water resist simply draining downward.

That longer contact allowed evaporation to continue for hours. The cooling effect lasted up to 20 hours in some tests.

This matters because heat does not arrive all at once. Buildings face long hot afternoons, warm evenings and repeated sun exposure.

Testing A Cooler Building Skin

The team tested the tiles under infrared heating and periodic watering. The results showed a major temperature difference.

The temperature beneath the elephant-skin-inspired tiles stayed at 89.6 degrees Fahrenheit. Under cracked commercial stucco, it rose to 107.6 degrees.

Under non-cracked stucco, it reached 125.6 degrees. That difference shows how much water management can change surface heat.

The team also tested the idea on a small model building. Water was delivered in cycles, while heat came from an infrared lamp.

The new tiles spread and retained water better than commercial stucco. They kept the space beneath them cooler with the same water input.

A Simple Design With Big Potential

The technology may be useful because it does not rely on complex machinery. It uses common cement, a porous additive and designed crack patterns.

The researchers also showed that the mixture could be applied to large panels using hopper guns. That suggests a possible path toward on-site construction.

The system could one day work with automated watering. Sensors and forecasts could help decide when a building needs cooling.

“Now that we understand how water moves through these patterned tiles, we can start treating water as something we manage very precisely instead of simply spraying more of it,” Yu said. “By combining these materials with weather forecasts and automated water delivery systems, we could supply just enough water, exactly where and when it’s needed, to maximize cooling while minimizing water use.”

That kind of control matters in hot, dry regions where water is limited.

Rethinking How Cities Stay Livable

The study offers a different way to think about buildings. Instead of sealing structures away from nature, materials could work with natural processes.

“Extreme heat is already the deadliest climate-related hazard, and we’ve spent decades trying to seal buildings off from the environment,” Aviv said. “If we can design materials that work with natural processes instead of against them, we can start to rethink how cities stay livable.”

The tiles are not a complete replacement for air conditioning. People will still need active cooling during dangerous heat.

But passive cooling can reduce the heat load on buildings. That may lower energy demand and make indoor spaces safer.

In a hotter world, even simple cooling gains can matter.

Practical Implications Of The Research

This research could help buildings stay cooler while using less energy. By lowering surface temperatures, elephant-skin-inspired tiles may reduce the need for mechanical air conditioning.

The technology may also help cities fight extreme heat. Cooler roofs and façades can reduce heat buildup on building surfaces and may ease pressure during heat waves.

The design could be especially valuable in dry climates, where evaporative cooling works well. With smart watering systems, buildings could use only the amount of water needed for cooling.

For humanity, the benefit is healthier, more livable cities. Extreme heat already threatens vulnerable people around the world. Materials that cool passively could help protect homes, schools, workplaces and public spaces while cutting energy use.

Dig deeper into passive cooling and climate-adaptive building materials

These resources examine evaporative cooling, radiative cooling and emerging materials designed to lower building temperatures without relying entirely on conventional air conditioning.

Advanced evaporative cooling materials: From designs to applications: Reviews the materials, structures and physical mechanisms being developed for passive evaporative cooling across buildings, electronics and other thermal-management applications. (Progress in Materials Science, 2025)

Passive isothermal film with self-switchable radiative cooling-driven water sorption layer for arid climate applications: Describes a passive material that combines radiative cooling with water-driven thermal processes to regulate temperature under extreme dry-climate conditions. (Nature Communications, 2024)

Humidity-tolerant porous polymer coating for passive daytime radiative cooling: Demonstrates a scalable porous coating designed to retain passive radiative-cooling performance across a wider range of environmental humidity conditions. (Nature Communications, 2024)

A biomass-derived material for passive radiative cooling: Examines a sustainable porous material that combines high solar reflectance with thermal emission to achieve passive cooling without external energy. (Nature Reviews Materials, 2024)

IEA EBC Annex 80: Summarizes an international research effort examining resilient passive and active strategies for reducing building overheating and cooling demand. (U.S. Department of Energy, 2020)

Research findings are available online in the journal Advanced Materials.

articles.title: Technically, This Cluster of Cabins Is a Single Home
articles.summary: The prefab structure in Paredes, Portugal, is stitched together at the edges to form a long, offset plan.
articles.content:
The prefab structure in Paredes, Portugal, is stitched together at the edges to form a long, offset plan.

Houses We Love: Every day we feature a remarkable space submitted by our community of architects, designers, builders, and homeowners. Have one to share? Post it here.

Project Details:

Location: Paredes, Portugal

Architect: Diogo Aguiar Studio / @diogoguiarstudio

Footprint: 2,152 square feet

Builder: Grupo Grandys

Builder: Somaia

Structural and Civil Engineer: PENREA

Photographer: Fernando Guerra

Photographer: Valentina Vagena

From the Architect: "House Over the Hills began with a simple request: to live differently. Close enough to the city to remain connected, yet far enough from its noise, density and concrete to recover something increasingly rare—silence. Set among the hills of Aguiar de Sousa, the house does not attempt to conquer the landscape. Its position, orientation and shifting roofline emerge from what was already there: the slope of the land, the distant silhouette of the mountains and, above all, the trees. The architecture establishes a precise order within this setting without making that order too visible.

"The exact level at which the house meets the terrain was therefore as important as its form. Approaching from the road, the building gradually reveals itself through its roofs rather than presenting a conventional facade. From within, that same decision brings the horizon into an almost continuous relationship with domestic life. The house was not placed where it could command the best view, but where architecture and landscape could most convincingly share the same ground.

"A modular timber system provides the house with its underlying discipline. Modules advance, retreat and change height, producing courtyards, shelter and unexpected spatial tensions. What begins as constructional logic becomes a sequence of compression, release, and discovery. This modularity also allows the program to resist a fixed idea of family life. Alongside the main dwelling, three independent units can operate autonomously or be absorbed into the household as circumstances change. Here, flexibility is understood less as movable architecture than as the capacity of a strong structure to accommodate different lives.

"Timber was chosen from an initial commitment to lower-impact construction, but its contribution goes beyond environmental performance. Its lightness enabled a precise relationship with the ground; its warmth, acoustic character, and tactility give the interiors a quality of comfort that is difficult to quantify but immediately understood by the body.

"Inside, the landscape is never reduced to a view. Openings placed at different heights allow branches, moving shadows, and changing light to enter the rooms throughout the day. The trees become part of the architecture’s choreography, making the house slightly different from one hour to the next. This relationship also changes the meaning of enclosure. Some openings address the distant mountains; others deliberately frame something much closer: a trunk, a patch of sky, the shadow of foliage crossing a timber wall. The house oscillates between distance and intimacy, between the scale of the territory and that of the body. Perhaps its most important landscape is not the one seen through the largest window, but the one that moves quietly across the interior."

articles.title: The Fascinating Science of How We Think Not with the Brain But with the World
articles.summary: "By reaching beyond the brain... we are able to focus more intently, comprehend more deeply, and create more imaginatively — to entertain ideas that would be literally unthinkable by the brain alone."
articles.content:
“By reaching beyond the brain… we are able to focus more intently, comprehend more deeply, and create more imaginatively — to entertain ideas that would be literally unthinkable by the brain alone.”

“Our minds are all threaded together,” the young Virginia Woolf wrote in her diary at the dawn of the twentieth century, “and all the world is mind.” Meanwhile in Spain, the middle-aged Santiago Ramón y Cajal was birthing a new science that would both greatly expand our knowledge of the brain and greatly contract our understanding of the mind. Over the following half-century, in its noble effort to render comprehensible what William James so poetically termed the “blooming and buzzing confusion” of consciousness, neuroscience would become both a great leap forward and a great leap back. Again and again, its illuminating but incomplete findings would be aggrandized and oversimplified into a sort of neo-phrenology that incarcerates some of our most expansive human experiences and capacities — love and grief, intelligence and imagination — in particular brain regions with particular neural firing patterns.

A century later and half a millennium after Descartes cleaved Western consciousness into its disembodied dualism, we are only just beginning to reckon with the growing understanding that consciousness is a full-body phenomenon, perhaps even a beyond-body phenomenon.

In The Extended Mind: The Power of Thinking Outside the Brain (public library), Annie Murphy Paul explores the most thrilling frontiers of this growing understanding, fusing a century of scientific studies with millennia of first-hand experience from the lives and letters of great artists, scientists, inventors, and entrepreneurs. Challenging our cultural inheritance of thinking that thinking takes place only inside the brain, she illuminates the myriad ways in which we “use the world to think” — from the sensemaking language of gestures that we acquire as babies long before we can speak concepts to the singular fuel that time in nature provides for the brain’s most powerful associative network.

Paul distills this recalibration of understanding:

Thinking outside the brain means skillfully engaging entities external to our heads — the feelings and movements of our bodies, the physical spaces in which we learn and work, and the minds of the other people around us — drawing them into our own mental processes. By reaching beyond the brain to recruit these “extra-neural” resources, we are able to focus more intently, comprehend more deeply, and create more imaginatively — to entertain ideas that would be literally unthinkable by the brain alone.

Even our metaphors for the mind have taken us further and further from our essential nature as creatures shaped by our environment and our interactions with other creatures, dishonoring Rachel Carson’s science-rooted poetic insight that “there is in us a deeply seated response to the natural universe, which is part of our humanity.” We left Plato’s cave of consciousness and, corralled by Descartes and the Industrial Revolution, reduced the mind to the brain, then reduced the brain to a machine, explaining its workings by drawing analogies to the technology of the hour: The brain was a loom, the brain was a telegraph, the brain was a computer.

In what remains one of the most inspired metaphors in the history of science, Paul renders the mind as a magpie — that evolutionary cousin of the crows and ravens, known for its uncommon intelligence and its ability to make messy yet elaborate nests out of whatever its environment has to offer.

Considering how profoundly this analogy reframes our understanding of mental processes, she writes:

Thought happens not only inside the skull but out in the world, too; it’s an act of continuous assembly and reassembly that draws on resources external to the brain. For another: the kinds of materials available to “think with” affect the nature and quality of the thought that can be produced. And last: the capacity to think well — that is, to be intelligent — is not a fixed property of the individual but rather a shifting state that is dependent on access to extra-neural resources and the knowledge of how to use them.

Reflecting on this mesh model of the mind — which mirrors what we have been learning about how trees “think” and “feel” over the past half century — Paul adds:

We extend beyond our limits, not by revving our brains like a machine or bulking them up like a muscle — but by strewing our world with rich materials, and by weaving them into our thoughts.

One major aspect of this extended mind is our capacity for interoception — an awareness of the internal sensations of the body that gives us a kind of non-conscious knowledge, which we might term intuition but which is rooted in concrete embodied experience and somatic pattern-recognition. We might not detect the signals consciously, but we respond to the information they carry.

Paul writes:

When a potentially relevant pattern is detected, it’s our interoceptive faculty that tips us off: with a shiver or a sigh, a quickening of the breath or a tensing of the muscles. The body is rung like a bell to alert us to this useful and otherwise inaccessible information. Though we typically think of the brain as telling the body what to do, just as much does the body guide the brain with an array of subtle nudges and prods. (One psychologist has called this guide our “somatic rudder.”) Researchers have even captured the body in mid-nudge, as it alerts its inhabitant to the appearance of a pattern that she may not have known she was looking for.

It is a curious notion, referring to ourselves — and our selves — as “inhabitants” of our bodies. I am reminded of Whitman (then again, I am frequently reminded of Whitman):

“And if the body were not the soul, what is the soul?”

And Whitman again, contemplating “the fathomless human brain” to go on asking:

“And what is reason? and what is love? and what is life?”

In the remainder of The Extended Mind, Paul goes on to explore the three most intriguing areas of growing understanding as we reorient our minds to our brains and bodies: embodied cognition (the empirical counterpart to the Austrian playwright and poet Thomas Bernhard’s observation that “there is nothing more revealing than to see a thinking person walking, just as there is nothing more revealing than to see a walking person thinking”), situated cognition (the empirical counterpart to the Scottish mountaineer and poet Nan Shepherd’s observation that “place and a mind may interpenetrate till the nature of both is altered”), and distributed cognition (the empirical echo of Woolf’s insight that “all the world is mind”) — ideas affirming quantum pioneer Erwin Schrödinger’s startling and stunningly reasoned statement that “the over-all number of minds is just one.”

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

articles.title: Maru Table
articles.summary: Mililab The post Maru Table appeared first on Leibal.
articles.content:
In Tokyo, design studio Mililab built the Maru table so its solid oak top holds under a millimeter of flex in normal use, a tolerance reached by kiln-drying the wood twice before any cutting begins.

The table is round, sized to standard dining height and built to pair with the studio’s Yume chair and Ishi stool. It seats four to six people without designating a head of the table or a corner seat, a difference from the rectangular tables the same seating count usually implies. The oak base carries the top’s weight straight down rather than out toward the edges, which is what keeps the top from flexing.

The base is where the geometry does its real work. The shaped oak legs flare outward as they rise, becoming the tabletop itself rather than meeting it at a joint. The edge that results follows a superellipsoid profile, curved enough to read as slender from across a room while staying rounded enough not to bite into a forearm resting against it.

Production splits the labor between machine and hand. CNC cutting takes the major dimensions out of solid North American oak selected to FAS grade or better, and the base structure is checked joint by joint before the two pieces are assembled. From there the table is hand-shaped and hand-sanded through progressive grits, a process the studio runs for nineteen to twenty-five days before finishing begins.

The table ships flat-pack with the tools and instructions needed for assembly, arriving under delivery-duty-paid terms across thirty-four countries and backed by a five-year structural warranty.

articles.title: On Self-Belief and Risking Everything
articles.summary: Ann Tashi Slater talks with writer Sigrid Nunez about writing as a between-state, being death-haunted, and why she should have become an animal trainer. The post On Self-Belief and Risking Everything appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist…
articles.content:
Between-States: Conversations About Bardo and Life

In Tibetan Buddhism, “bardo” is a between-state. The passage from death to rebirth is a bardo, as well as the journey from birth to death. The conversations in “Between-States” explore bardo concepts like acceptance, interconnectedness, and impermanence in relation to children and parents, marriage and friendship, and work and creativity, illuminating the possibilities for discovering new ways of seeing and finding lasting happiness as we travel through life.

***

In a new collection of stories, It Will Come Back to You, Sigrid Nunez explores between-states, from life stages like adolescence and aging to the reversals that day-to-day existence brings. In one of the most powerful stories in the collection, “Airport Story,” a woman ends up stranded and disoriented in an airport when her flight is delayed. 

“So innocently, so unexpectedly, the woman loses her sense of identity through no fault of her own,” Nunez says, “because of this strange but totally ordinary situation in an airport. You’re going along and you think, ‘This is life, this is me, this is how things are,’ and suddenly it’s like you leave the ground. You’re walking on air and you don’t know how you got there. You also don’t know how and when you’re going to come down.”

Born in 1951 in New York City, Nunez has written nine novels and a memoir, Sempre Susan, about her relationship with Susan Sontag. Nunez’s novel The Friend (2018) won the National Book Award for Fiction and was made into a film with Naomi Watts and Bill Murray. What Are You Going Through (2020) was adapted by director Pedro Almodóvar into The Room Next Door, starring Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore. It Will Come Back to You is Nunez’s first collection and brings together stories published over the last thirty years. In addition to the National Book Award, her honors include a Guggenheim Fellowship and the Rome Prize in Literature. 

Nunez talked with me about writing as a between-state, being death-haunted, and why she should have become an animal trainer.

*

Your work is often about liminality, times when we find ourselves in some kind of intermediate state. When do you feel in between? The first thing that comes to mind is that I feel very much in bardo when I’m writing. It’s a desirable state of suspension, one where I forget myself. The painter Philip Guston, quoting John Cage, said that when you’re in your art studio and you start painting, everyone is in there with you: the past, your friends, enemies, the art world, and, above all, your own ideas. But as you continue painting, they start to leave, one by one, until you’re left completely alone. Then, if you’re lucky, even you leave. 

As we travel in the bardo between birth and death, the choices we make influence our trajectory. How did you shape your path as a writer, from when you were just starting out to the tremendous success you’re having now? It took a long time for things to happen. I wasn’t getting published, wasn’t making money. There was a certain amount of humiliation to endure. I would go to the dentist and he’d say, “Oh, you’re still writing? Haven’t you been working on that book for about fifteen years?” (No, I wasn’t working all that time on one book.) Once I was at a dinner party and someone said, “What do you do?” When I said I was a writer, this woman asked, “What name do you write under?” In front of the whole table!

Was your family supportive? My parents were quite reasonably worried about how I expected to make a living. And somebody I was close to and trusted, a boyfriend who was a psychiatrist and who really liked the work I was doing, said, “Sometimes you have to give up a dream in order to move on.” By that time, I was in my late 30s. Things were going very badly, and I was in tears a lot. 

When he said that, you didn’t think you might give up? No. I knew it was a loving thing to say and he wasn’t trying to sabotage me. And, of course, he was not wrong, but as it turned out, about me, he was wrong. I knew writing was what I was supposed to be doing.

The Tibetan Book of the Dead urges us to embrace our authentic nature in bardo, to live in alignment with our true selves. How did you stay the course despite the difficulties you encountered? For me, it was a question of self-belief. I became less and less risk-averse, and I thought, “Well, I’m not going to stop now.”

Part of it was something that didn’t occur to me until a few years ago, when I was doing an interview for The Paris Review. My father, who was Chinese-Panamanian, was a gambler, not unto ruination, but he gambled the way many Asian men gamble. I realized I’d inherited that trait, that it was in my DNA to dare to keep writing even when I wasn’t having any success and so much time was passing. In other words, I was willing to gamble with my future and risk everything in the hope that I’d reach my goal in the end.

I just kept going, and opportunities and encouragement started to come: a story accepted by a little magazine, some small award, a person I greatly respected saying of something I wrote, “This is really good.”

And then you started getting your books published. My first book, A Feather on the Breath of God, was very, very, very hard to get published. It was rejected by one editor after another; I can’t recall just how many. It finally got accepted when I was 42, and it came out when I was 44, which is considered quite late for a debut.

From that time, I made an effort to organize everything around my writing. It helped to be in a place like New York—I found flexible jobs proofreading, teaching ESL, whatever. I took time off to go to residencies, where I’d meet other writers who were supportive, telling me that my writing was good. 

But I should give credit here to Susan Sontag, who came into my life after I graduated from the MFA program at Columbia. For her, writing was like a religious vocation, an exalted and even heroic profession, and the best job in the world. A person who wanted to write had to be super serious, ready and willing to make large sacrifices, without the promise or expectation of money or fame. 

From her I felt that I was being given permission to do this unjustifiable thing of devoting my life to writing, while everyone else was concerned with how I was going to make a living and when I was going to find a husband and settle down.

Do you think you’ll stop writing someday? I’m thinking of stopping. Or limiting it, not writing as much as I have been, because it’s so all-consuming.

When Philip Roth stopped writing fiction, he started going to concerts, seeing his friends. Do you feel drawn to that? I do, to be able to do all these things that people do when they retire. Sontag was appalled by such an idea. The word “retire” made her very sick. But that’s because all the time that she was writing, she was going to concerts and movies and out with her friends! She was famous for that. But I never could do it all. I feel like I’ve missed a lot. 

The bardo teachings are about awareness that everything changes and ends, including us. Is there a point at which you became aware of mortality? I’ve always been death-haunted. Part of the reason for that is that my mother was raised in Nazi Germany and came of age during the Second World War. She met my father when he was serving over there with the occupying forces, and he brought her here, to Brooklyn.

Ours wasn’t a religious household, so we kids didn’t hear anything about people seeing each other again in heaven. Death was just a plain boiled fact of life.

My mother had seen a lot of death, and even when we kids were very young, she’d tell us stories about people who were killed in the war. She would also speak matter-of-factly about the deaths of people in our community. “Oh, Mrs. Rodriguez’s father died,” she’d say. Almost as if it were no big thing. There was never any discussion of what death meant. And ours wasn’t a religious household, so we kids didn’t hear anything about people seeing each other again in heaven. Death was just a plain boiled fact of life. 

You say death haunts you. Do you mean that you fear it? Death is always on my mind, and always part of my work. But I think of myself as somebody who’s not afraid of death. The idea of moving on has not terrified me yet. If you reach a certain age, you can feel like you’ve lived your given life, and though, of course, there’s more you could see and do, you can go in peace. 

Though, to be clear, I’m very afraid of the way we die. Sontag was an example of how you don’t want to die. Kicking and screaming. Resistant to the point that she insisted on radical treatments that it was understood had almost no chance of working. I don’t have what she had, this overwhelming terror of the dark. But who knows how I’ll feel when it happens to me. I’ve heard people say they’re not afraid, and then when they’re dying, they feel completely different.

My father was a philosopher and a physician, and he wasn’t afraid of dying. What he feared was reaching the end of his life with regrets over not having lived it. Now that I’m 75, I think about regrets. I’m at a time when it’s natural to look back and think about what didn’t happen, whereas before I could think, “Well, such-and-such a thing could still happen.”

Some of my regrets are silly, like, “I always wanted to learn how to juggle but never did.” I also wish I’d learned more languages. I wish I’d spent more time in nature, and more time traveling. I also regret not having had more animals in my life. 

You couldn’t have a pet now? The problem is that the cats I used to have lived a long time, and losing them was terrible. Their final days were too much, they both suffered a lot, and I can’t go through that again, especially not alone. 

But when I think about what I might have done if I weren’t a writer—what would have made me a much happier, more fulfilled person—it’s doing some kind of work with animals. I believe I would have been a good trainer or caretaker of animals, because I’m patient with animals, much more so than with people, and I’ve always loved them a lot.

When I was having an extremely hard time trying to make it as a writer, a friend of mine brought up the “animal lady,” who was a regular on Johnny Carson’s Tonight Show and who used to bring various live animals on the show to talk about. My friend said, “This is what you should have done with your life. This is who you are.” I thought there was a lot of truth to that. 

I feel that particular missed chance more than I regret not having had children. Because even though I love children, I would never have had a child as a single person, ever. I would always have had to be with somebody, and no one I was ever with was somebody I wanted to have children with—or who wanted children himself. So I don’t think of it as something I regret not having done, because it wasn’t meant to happen.

The Dalai Lama says that, fundamentally, we all want to be happy. This is our common human bond as we travel in the bardo of life, whatever our circumstances. Do you feel happy now? Like so many people, I’m obsessed with current events, the sense of a world spinning out of control. The craziness and cruelty and corruption. Sometimes I feel like I’m drowning in it.

The world has been troubled my whole life because the world is always troubled, but things are different now. I keep expecting ever more terrible things to happen: Somebody will drop a nuclear bomb, hackers will create chaos through massive cyberattacks, destructive weather events will keep getting worse, and on and on.

People I know who are my age say, “Who wants to spend the last part of their life in this mess?” But I’m able to write, and when I’m writing, I’m able to feel like I’m doing what I should be doing despite all the bad things happening in the world.

It’s important, as well, to have a sense of humor, to still be able to see the comic aspects in things, and to be around other people who can do that too. 

The Dalai Lama is a wonderful example. He’s suffered tremendous loss, yet he calls himself a “professional laugher.” He loves joking around. That’s the way it should be. There’s nothing more human than that.

The post On Self-Belief and Risking Everything appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.

articles.title: Boulder’s proposed 2027 budget would cut 13 filled jobs and trim pool hours
articles.summary: The city manager’s recommended budget seeks to close a projected $6.3 million General Fund gap through staffing and service cuts and by using revenue from voter-approved taxes to cover more expenses. The post Boulder’s proposed 2027 budget …
articles.content:
The Boulder City Council this week is scheduled to begin debating the city manager’s proposed 2027 budget, which reflects an ongoing effort to address rising costs and revenue growth that has failed to keep pace.

The proposed $552 million budget marks an increase from last year, largely due to new capital investments. It also comes with notable staffing cuts to help close a $6.3 million gap in the General Fund, the city’s largest fund and a key source of money for a wide range of services.

The proposal would cut about 24 full-time-equivalent positions, including 13 filled positions that would result in layoffs. The staffing cuts would save about $3 million, according to a city official. 

It is the second year in a row the city manager has proposed cutting staffing levels, though last year only three of the eliminated positions were filled. 

“Decisions that impact people are never easy,” City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde said in a news release. “At the same time, during challenging times, we must ensure that our constrained resources are going to the services our community counts on most.” 

The filled positions slated to be cut include three in innovation and technology. The city also plans to eliminate its photo enforcement van program and instead rely on traffic patrols and automated red-light and speed-on-green cameras. Ending the program would eliminate seven filled civilian positions in the Boulder Police Department. The city plans to hire officers for other roles. 

The cuts follow several years of slow revenue growth. Sales tax revenue, the city’s largest single source of money, has come in below projections. The city has also lowered its property tax revenue projections because of state legislation that reduced assessment rates.

For the first time since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic, the city manager last year recommended cuts to General Fund spending to help close a $7.5 million shortfall in the 2026 budget. To address the current gap, she has asked all departments to identify ongoing 4% reductions, with an emphasis on permanent cuts.

The city manager is also proposing to shift costs out of the General Fund and into other funds, some of which voters approved for specific purposes. For example, the  proposed budget would use open space money to pay for a larger share of Boulder Fire-Rescue’s Wildland Unit and revenue from the Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Distribution Tax to pay for more parks and recreation services.

Residents may also see service reductions. The budget would cut hours at Scott Carpenter Pool and indoor pools in the city’s recreation centers. City officials have already said they lack the money to operate Spruce Pool beyond 2027.

The budget still includes several new investments, among them nearly $20 million toward the development of 155 units of affordable housing at the Alpine-Balsam site, the city’s largest affordable housing development, and an additional $300,000 to reduce wildfire risk for homes and other properties. The city is also planning to increase pay for city employees, including 5% raises for the police and fire unions and 4% for other city staff. Some seasonal workers will receive additional pay under the city’s minimum wage.

The plan also relies on new or increased revenue. The city expects to collect an estimated $3 million in 2027 through a Transportation Maintenance Fee, charged to homes and commercial buildings, along with revenue from increased utility rates for water, wastewater and stormwater services. The city also plans to raise its recreational marijuana retail tax from 3.5% to 5.5%, an administrative change that officials said does not require voter approval.

The proposal comes as Boulder’s budget is front and center in this fall’s city election. Voters will consider a ballot measure intended to help cover major capital costs, while candidates for mayor and city council debate the city’s spending priorities and how to respond to slower revenue growth.

The Boulder City Council will hold a first reading on Oct. 1, followed by a final public hearing and vote Oct. 15.

articles.title: As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?
articles.summary: When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’”…
articles.content:
When the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that new and unprecedented reality.

Another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center launched the New Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the New Map of Life. What are you seeing?

LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and said, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”

KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the New Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot quickly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering new products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

It’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

We have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

This story was originally published by Stanford Center on Longevity. Read the original article.

articles.title: Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped
articles.summary: The post Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped appeared first on NOEMA.
articles.content:
We’ve long been ensorcelled by the passage of time. Puckered leaves fluttering from the spidery arms of barren trees. Grains of sand tumbling through the delicate neck of an hourglass. A curved cornice perched over a snow-covered mountain, awaiting an avalanche to bring it down. These evocative emblems of seasons, hours, and the vicissitudes they leave in their wake speak to the bittersweet relationship we’ve cultivated with this unit of measurement.

Whether in Proustian reveries, digital photo libraries, or the watchful doppelgänger that gazes out at us each morning, ever-so-slightly altered, we’re inclined to a tender wistfulness toward time — the persistent awareness that, however fast or slow, it’s forever slipping through our fingers.

But lately, our relationship to the months, years and decades that landscape our lives has shifted in some unsettling ways. Instead of regarding the passage of time with introspection or melancholy, many of us now observe it with a mounting sense of alarm. 

You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence that we are experiencing a metaphysical crack-up around time. There’s a growing conviction among people from all walks of life that time is moving faster than it did several decades ago — or even prior to the Covid pandemic. While this belief crept into the zeitgeist like a sly, slinking fog, the refrains are now so pervasive that they’ve started to supplant idle chatter on the weather. Our focus has shifted from rejoicing in cloudless days or grousing over gloomy skies to fixating on the dizzying speed at which our lives are hurtling by. 

This is particularly evident on sites like Reddit, where users now regularly commiserate over how rapidly the years are passing. A farmer whose work cycles alongside the seasons “can’t believe how fast this year has gone.” A middle school teacher recounts how she finds herself “having these conversations with students … who are perturbed by the speed of life.”  Perhaps most tellingly, for a programmer, the “pandemic years blurred together, and everything after feels compressed, like one long season instead of separate years.” Civilizational events, including not only Covid but also climate change, large-scale armed conflict and the rise of AI “have piled up so quickly that it feels like we’re living through multiple decades at once.”

In recent years, these stray observations have coalesced into a chorus. Everyone from Boomers to Zoomers is mystified at how the passage of time has sped up, and feels disoriented by the strange velocity that’s colored how we’re living through the 2020s. But to hear these stifled laments is also to observe the absurdity of contemporary American life: While so many of us agree that our relationship to time has been warped, our collective response has been to shake it off and move on. It’s as though we all started losing our depth perception at the same time — crashing into road medians, pratfalling down staircases — and instead of resolving to rectify the predicament, we’ve simply resigned ourselves to daily collisions and collapses.

In some ways, the scale of this phenomenon resembles an episode of mass cognitive dissonance, or even a population-level folie à deux. It’s worth asking if something about our internal mechanisms for gauging the passage of time has changed — or been irrevocably thrown out of sync with human timekeeping and the atomic clocks we’ve structured civilization around for nearly a century. Or, alternatively, perhaps the pandemic spoiled our capacity to judge duration, expanding and contracting our sense of time over and over until the fabric grew loose and rippled, an undifferentiated mass of fibers stretched into a form we no longer recognize.

A Theory Of Relativity

Scientists and academics have been grappling with some of these questions since the 19th century. In the 1890s, renowned French philosopher Paul Janet proposed that human beings experience time in proportion to their age. When we’re 10 years old, one year is fully 10% of our entire lifetimes; as a result, we process it with slow, substantive vividness. When we’re 50 years old, on the other hand, that same year represents only 2% of our lives, and we experience it with corresponding ephemerality and diminished gravitas. Janet’s theory would come to be known as “logarithmic time perception,” a reference to the measurement scale that represents mathematical figures proportionately (it’s sometimes referred to as the “time alive” theory).

William James picked up where Janet left off, positing in “Principles of Psychology” that time moves more slowly for young people, who slingshot themselves into fresh experiences every day. “Apprehension is vivid, retentiveness strong, and our recollections of that time, like those of a time spent in rapid and interesting travel, are of something intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out,” he writes.

James argues that the absorbing episodes children and teenagers so often find themselves in give the brain more to chew on — both in the moment and long after the moment’s passed. Because their exploits are consistently novel and stimulating, young people have the retrospective sensation that those specific intervals of time were fuller, deeper, more robust.

As we grow older, however, we become more immersed in patterns and routines, without the same opportunities to process new information, foster fresh skills or feel our way through unfamiliar circumstances that galvanize our intellects. We’re living by rote, so to speak, and our consciousness slides into a more dulled, dampened state. As a result, James notes, “the days and the weeks smooth themselves out in recollection to contentless units, and the years grow hollow and collapse.”

Though James was writing before the fields of neuroscience and psychology were even established — Freud had yet to publish his first book — his insights have been embraced by researchers more than a century later. Many of them now argue that the way we gauge time is inextricably linked to how active and engaged our brains are, and the extent to which we form memories.

When we’re seeing, hearing, touching and tasting exotic sights, sounds, surfaces and foods that arouse our senses, we’re far more likely to lay down new memories. Those recollections inform how we retrospectively evaluate the passage of time, giving it that languorous, “long-drawn-out” quality James described. “We only remember things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them,” Luke Jones, a psychologist at the University of Manchester, explained to me. “And your retrospective perception of duration is based on memory.”

But while we’ve long established that humans perceive time in an elastic, subjective way, that knowledge could not have prepared us for the Covid pandemic. That generational event bowed and buckled the way so many of us experience those hourglasses and cornices, swapping out placid reflection for consternation and dread. Over three years of lockdowns, quarantines and the claustrophobic monotony they inspired, countless Americans told anyone who would listen how different time felt to them. The weeks and months, we stammered, felt “stretched,” “warped,” “blurred.”

In 2023, researchers at Baylor University set out to legitimize these anecdotes. A team of sociologists published a study using Gallup data collected at the height of the pandemic to analyze how people perceived time during the period. The authors found that Americans experienced “time disorientation” in multiple directions, with time speeding up, slowing down and days blending together to the point of indistinguishability.

Another study of Uruguayan university students, published in “Time & Society” in 2022, found that 80% of students surveyed felt time had either sped up or slowed down during the pandemic. These findings were replicated in other parts of the world, including Argentina and Iraq. The co-authors of the “Time & Society” paper also noted an intriguing irony: In instances where excessive free time caused by lockdowns or other public health measures led to boredom, “time would be slow in the moment, but looking back on the experience retrospectively, people would feel that time flew.” 

This points to a crucial aspect of time perception, one that continues to captivate me: We gauge the speed of time based on one set of factors in the moment — how engaged or stimulated we are — while using a distinct set of criteria to evaluate it retrospectively (the degree to which we formed memories). People trapped in their homes during the pandemic with little to do suffered a worst-case scenario, temporally speaking: the emptiness of their days slowed them to a crawl, while the insipid repetition of their experiences yielded few memories, causing wide swaths of time to, as James puts it, “grow hollow and collapse.”

When I spoke to Marc Wittmann, one of the 2022 study’s co-authors and a time perception researcher at the Institute for Frontier Areas in Psychology and Mental Health in Germany, he explained that the lack of distinct markers during the pandemic made each day look exactly alike, contributing to time disorientation. “Every day was the same,” he said. “Monday used to be the day you went skating, Tuesday was the day you spent with your friends. We used to have something associated with each day.” But all of this disappeared during global lockdowns, he said. Wittmann calls this “Blursday.”

The surge in time disorientation so many of us experienced during the pandemic came to be known as the “2020 effect.” The abrupt upheaval and subsequent tedium of restrictive, repetitive routines in those years led to the sensation of days bleeding into each other, time “stretching” and people losing the ability to recall events sequentially — as though our memories were shuffled and rearranged during a game of three-card monte.

But the most relevant question in 2026 isn’t whether the pandemic influenced how we experience time. A raft of academic papers demonstrate that it clearly did. The question now is whether our perception of time ever snapped back to the way it was before that generational event. 

The Internal Clock Fallacy

To determine why our internal clocks sped up over the past few years, it helps to understand exactly what we mean by “internal clocks.” For years, time perception researchers have been trying to explain how human beings subjectively gauge duration. But it’s proven to be a stubborn riddle. One reason for this is that we have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time. Instead, as one 2016 paper puts it, “Psychological time is an abstraction, a construct or epiphenomenon of our mind’s functioning that we create in order to explain the coherence of events.”

Nevertheless, researchers were convinced for years that humans possessed a specific mechanism for measuring time — a theory referred to as the “internal clock model.” Though the model served as a convenient explanation for how humans tell time, scientists eventually grew skeptical of it. “Back then, there was a very anthropocentric model that was suspiciously similar to actual man-made clocks,” said Dean Buonomano, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You have some oscillator ticking away at some frequency, and then counting the time units, much like clocks work.” Another problem with the internal clock model was that scientists struggled to find hard evidence for its existence. As Warrick Roseboom, a psychologist at the University of Sussex, told me, “Researchers were just like, ‘Oh, you have a clock in your brain. We just need to find where the clock in your brain is.’”

But scientists never found the clock, and for some the model lost its credibility. Meanwhile, Roseboom and other academics began exploring alternative theories. In 2022, he and several colleagues at the University of Sussex published the results of a study that showed participants short videos to determine whether there was a relationship between the way we process the world around us and how we gauge the passage of time.

In the experiment, the amount of activity the videos elicited in participants’ brains was strongly correlated with their subjective sense of how much time passed. When the participants detected more happening in the videos, it triggered large changes in brain activity associated with visual processing, creating the sensation that more time had gone by. Roseboom and his co-authors concluded that we tell time based on “the accumulation of salient changes in the perceptual processing hierarchy” — or, as co-author Maxine Sherman said when the paper was published, “the brain just ‘counts’ how much ‘stuff’ has happened, which is very intuitive.” 

One of the paper’s key takeaways is that our perception of time isn’t based on any fixed sense of duration. We do not, in fact, have an internal clock measuring minutes, hours and days. Instead, we use our external environment as a proxy for the passage of time. The more “stuff” our sensory cortex is picking up on, the more time we register as passing. 

This new way of looking at time perception could shed light on why so many people feel like time is speeding up today. We’re inundated with videos, images, notifications and a cavalcade of content 24 hours a day, forcing our brains to contend with far more information than they needed to 10 or 20 years ago. 

When I reached out to James Hyman, a neuroscientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, he felt that applying Roseboom and his co-authors’ new theory of time perception to our current media ecosystem explained why so many people now feel flummoxed by the speed of their lives. “We’re constantly moving onto the next thing,” he said. “And the more things that we experience that cause us to move forward, well, if our brains are only able to tell time by counting things, then we’re jamming lots more things in there.” When we’re flooded with text, images and glowing blue light, our brains are tricked into speeding up the internal proxy mechanisms they use for measuring time. As a result, time feels like it’s moving faster and faster.

But the casino-like frenzy of our digital environments is only part of the reason our perception of time is changing. Remember that we assess duration from multiple vantage points, including retrospectively, when we gauge how much time we feel passed during a specific period. When we tell our spouse that “this week flew by,” we’re engaging in retrospective time perception. Arguably the most important variable in those judgments is memory — whether we formed them, how many we formed, how vivid they are. 

Memories are the trees, shrubs and undulating peaks that landscape our past, preventing it from hollowing out and collapsing in on itself. (Smooth and featureless as the interior of a spaceship, the pandemic had no landscape, and our memory of it collapsed accordingly.) Because of this variability, retrospective time perception is even more subjective than other forms of time judgment, given its outsized dependence on “things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them.” The memories that stem from those stimuli are our footprints in the snow, giving our past the solidity and verisimilitude that would otherwise blow away in the past’s enveloping whiteout. 

Our memories are the key to the central irony of our supersaturated world. Roseboom’s theory posits that time spent in an environment overflowing with visual information should feel long and robust. “You would think that because we’re paying more attention to more things, that retrospectively time should feel longer,” Jones noted. “But I think we’ve got the worst of all worlds.” Because while we encounter a glittering constellation of apps, games and videos beckoning us at every turn, eager to light up our sensory cortex, they’re not generating the indelible experiences crucial to forming memories. “When you get to the end of the day, you look back and there’s no meaningful content there. It’s just the same blur, the same stuff, and there’s nothing distinctive about it.”

Wittmann agrees that toggling between apps on our phone and numbing ourselves with Instagram reels can impoverish our retrospective perception of time. “When we’re on digital media, time passes very quickly,” he explained. “You lose yourself. You’re jumping around like mad in these apps, and you can’t put them into memory and later recall them, because the experiences just vanish.” 

Browsing, scrolling and swiping are more likely to quiet or even anesthetize our brains than activate them in the ways required to form memories. As a result, spending an hour on TikTok might feel like 10 or 15 minutes, because we don’t have any of the “intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out” sensations that give time depth and fullness. Instead, it all blends together in a turbulent vortex, overwhelming the senses rather than engaging them on the level necessary to endure over time. It’s easy to extrapolate this further and speculate how spending several hours a day on social media distorts our sense of time, giving us the impression that we were awake for just 12 or 13 hours of the day. Over months and years, surrendering this much time to our ersatz digital warrens can lead to a sense of deprivation — a feeling that years have been carved out of our lives.

According to Wittmann and other researchers, social media platforms are uniquely effective at short-circuiting our retrospective time perception. After spending time on these apps, the abstract field our mind’s eye draws from to make sense of recent experiences is left barren, devoid of the evocative wisps we integrate into the hazy memory palace that ultimately serves as our past. Instead, many of us are now confined to a permanent amnesiac present, one throbbing with artificial life but unable to fathom where it came from or where it’s going. 

Investigating The Time Warp 

The collective sense that time is moving faster today than it has in the past has gained enough traction for scientists to start taking notice. A group of European psychologists has teamed up to form Time Experience in Europe’s Digital Age, abbreviated as TIMED. This research consortium, which includes some of the top time-perception researchers in Germany, Spain, Switzerland and the U.K., is using interviews, questionnaires and experiments to explore how our perception of time is influenced by how we use technology.

TIMED has spent the last three years collecting data from tens of thousands of study participants all over the world, and they’re now sharing the results of that project. In papers published so far, researchers have arrived at a number of important takeaways. First, people who spend more time on devices and social media platforms experience time passing more quickly. In one of their papers, Wittmann and his co-authors cited memory as a key factor in this correlation, with the use of digital technology limiting the breadth of people’s experiences and foreclosing on the events we most often remember.

“Routine activities such as repeatedly checking apps or prolonged online engagement for professional purposes could reduce the frequency of novel, embodied, and enactive experiences,” they wrote. “This, in turn, results in fewer rich or meaningful events being encoded in autobiographical memory. Consequently, such periods may retrospectively appear less eventful and more compressed, contributing to the feeling that time has passed quickly.”

Unsurprisingly, perhaps, researchers also found that excessive use of technological devices promoted a negative relationship with time. “Participants associated digital technology use with a loss of time, a desire to fill all time, a propensity to forget time and, as a result, a desire to gain greater control of time,” they wrote. Feeling that one’s relationship with time had spun out of control in turn spawned “feelings of guilt, shame, and a lack of self-control.”

Wittmann and his colleagues conducted qualitative interviews for TIMED, and some participants expressed frustration and even helplessness at how devices were transforming their sense of time. “What was really interesting to me was how people constantly talked about digital technology stealing their time,” Ruth Ogden, TIMED’s lead investigator, said. “One of the things that happens when you engage in doom scrolling and other forms of social media is you completely forget about time — time doesn’t exist anymore. So then you massively overextend how long you engage in these activities for.”

But Ogden doesn’t think that technology should be seen as the sole culprit for our warped perceptions of time. The strains in that relationship go deeper than memes, AI slop and infinite scroll, stemming from how modern society frames inert, unproductive states like boredom and “doing nothing.” In TIMED’s interviews, respondents also told Ogden and her colleagues they were uncomfortable with periods of inactivity and felt compelled to use their devices to fill every available gap in their schedule. “What we found through TIMED is that even when people have time, they don’t use it to do nothing,” she told me. “We live in a society that really values constantly being busy and constantly having something to do. We saw this in TIMED through people’s use of digital technology, where every bit of free time was spent on screens.”

If people were more comfortable with intervals that lacked so-called productivity — quiet longueurs, spells of boredom or periods of aimless reflection — they might stand a better chance of expanding and enriching the way they experience time. “It’s in those calm moments where we see a unique pattern of activity in the part of our brain responsible for helping to make our memories,” Hyman said. Those still, empty stretches are when we contemplate our immediate pasts, integrating them into the larger arc of our lives.

We know, however, that these states have been largely vaporized this decade — and only a seismic shift in our values and ideals stands a chance of reclaiming them. In Ogden’s eyes, the dilemma hinges on a simple question: “How do we get people back to being comfortable with doing very little and believing that doing little is not an indication of laziness?”

The Beauty Of Boredom

The stakes of this phenomenon can sometimes seem low. Feeling like time is speeding up is not a “kitchen table issue”; it won’t raise your taxes or make you go hungry. But the TIMED project has demonstrated that people who feel like they’re losing time are genuinely unhappy and even distressed about it. Members of Gen Z, in particular, don’t talk about the quickening pace of their lives with disinterested curiosity or frivolous bemusement — they lament it. When we lose our grip on the passage of time, it can feel like we’re also losing grip on our own lives. 

Western culture views time as a currency to be leveraged, channeled and optimized. The societal pressure to perform productivity at all times is so insistent and thrumming that many of us — myself included — have lost the ability to slow down and luxuriate in the inherent slowness of time, the way it oozes forward like honey slithering across a glass jar. When Aldous Huxley was asked about time by an interlocutor in “The Doors of Perception,” his reply was both simple and profound. “There seems to be plenty of it,” he said. Untethered from his ego and all the worldly attachments it clung to, Huxley was able to tap into the spaciousness of existence — an amplitude and abundance that’s permanent and inviolable, if only we still had the freedom to see it.

It’s true that technology has capitalized on this culture of synchronized compliance. The companies that manufacture our devices and make the programs that run on them have wedged themselves into this perverse relationship to productivity, offering the badges and motifs that signify a certain enterprising competence. As Jenny Odell points out in her book, “How to Do Nothing,” there’s a battle playing out “for our time, a colonization of the self by capitalist ideas of productivity and efficiency.” Through these products, we personify the ideals of practicality and industriousness.

The pandemic, too, eventually fed into the hungry zeitgeist of maximizing our output and sacrificing ourselves on the altar of “getting ahead.” The increased use of communications platforms like Slack, Teams and Zoom promoted a porousness between our work and home lives, allowing what Odell calls a “certain nervous feeling, of being overstimulated and unable to sustain a train of thought” to infiltrate spaces long insulated from them. 

This explains why many people feel that the way they experienced time during the pandemic never snapped back to how they processed it before Covid. In the aftermath, we became even more tethered to these platforms and other virtual spaces where productivity lingers at a low, insistent hum 24 hours a day. With our minds more anxious and overstimulated, our perception of time never had the chance to return to an earlier, more composed pace.

Further, trends that predated Covid resurfaced as though shot out of a cannon, and the ambient pressure to advance our lots at all costs imbued our culture with a mercenary quality. We were all racing to make more money, afford a home, secure a job, #YOLO at the live events we were unceremoniously robbed of. Amid this competitive turbulence — and the technologies that capitalized on our unease about it — everything started to move faster. 

If we accept this premise, then maybe the crisis of time speeding up is not as hopelessly irreversible as it often seems. According to the latest time perception research, the amount of information our brains engage with shapes our subjective sense of how fast time is moving. If we intentionally reduce the stimuli we’re exposing ourselves to in a given day or week, then our brains will gradually slow down. And if our brains slow down, then our perception of time will taper off, too. 

For their part, Ogden and other TIMED researchers feel that society has imposed too much responsibility on the individual to limit their use of technology. “Maybe it’s time that we shifted some of that onto the creators,” Ogden said. “The key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for, and how many people they can get on it for as long as possible. How do we flip that?” While we wait for those larger systemic changes, though, Ogden emphasized the importance of using our devices in a more intentional fashion. “What are you trying to get out of this digital technology use?” she asked. “You need to have an awareness of your own goals.”

In addition to modifying our own individual behavior, however, we also need to change the culture surrounding how we spend our time. That means coming to terms with the reality that boredom and “doing nothing” are neither shameful nor necessary evils. “There is huge value in doing nothing,” Ogden said. “We need to move away from thinking that it’s weird, lazy or slovenly.” Asked how she would spend a perfect holiday, Ogden described something very close to what people now labor so strenuously to avoid. “It would be to go and sit in a square in Italy with a nice glass of wine and watch the world go by.”

In his “Principles of Psychology,” William James invites us to participate in an experiment. “Close your eyes and simply wait to hear somebody tell you that a minute has elapsed,” he writes. The length of that single minute, he explains, will feel overwhelming. “You engulf yourself into its bowels as into those of that interminable first week of an ocean voyage, and find yourself wondering that history can have overcome many such periods in its course.” Those 60 seconds feel so full, James goes on, because “you attend so closely to the mere feeling of the time per se.” When our senses are engaged and stimulated, time is compressed, disguised, eclipsed. “The feeling of bare time,” however, “is the least stimulating experience we can have.”

We used to tolerate those interminable minutes standing in a crowded grocery line, gazing out the convex glass window of an airplane, waiting for the dull red digits on an oven timer to run down to zero. These are now the endangered species of our day-to-day lives. And they are far more valuable than we ever could have known.

The post Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped appeared first on NOEMA.
