articles.title: Nicolas Cage’s Malibu Home Has a Sink Hole—and Everything Else You Need to Know About This Week
articles.summary: Trump cuts funding to public parks, an NYC library launches a new craft supplies program, and more.
articles.content:
Trump cuts funding to public parks, an NYC library launches a new craft supplies program, and more.

  • A massive sinkhole opened outside Nicolas Cage’s Malibu home, prompting the beach city to declare a local emergency and issue evacuation orders to 31 homes. The collapsed road, which could worsen with high tides and rain, has hindered emergency personnel’s access, and gas has been shut off in the area. (The Los Angeles Times)

  • Trump’s policies, including "funding cuts, grant cancellations, and administrative delays," are stalling or shrinking park projects across the country, with underserved neighborhoods who are desperate for green spaces hit especially hard. In Queens, the proposed QueensWay lost most of a $117 million federal grant due to a provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill, leaving the High Line–esque project facing major downsizing. (Bloomberg)

  • The Brooklyn Public Library is launching its first craft library, where library cardholders can borrow art supplies for embroidery, bookbinding, metal stamping, screen printing, and more. The program lets New Yorkers test drive a hobby before investing in pricey supplies. (Gothamist)

  • In Corsica, an island region of France on the Mediterranean sea, separatists are bombing vacation homes as anger grows toward second homeowners who now own 37 percent of the island’s housing stock. Here’s how the attacks are intertwined with Corsica’s push for autonomy from France. (The New York Times)

  • A.I. altered real estate listings are fooling renters and buyers with larger, brighter-looking rooms, better views, and even fake fireplaces. Now, lawmakers, including Mayor Mamdani, are pushing brokers to disclose when listing photos have been digitally enhanced. Here’s why some realtors are embracing A.I. as a helpful tool, while others are sick of deceptive "real estate slop." (The New York Times)

Top photo by David Swanson / AFP via Getty Images

articles.title: SAR
articles.summary: Oskar Firek Architects The post SAR appeared first on Leibal.
articles.content:
SAR is a minimalist residence by the Kraków-based design studio, Oskar Firek Architects. Located in the Polish capital’s Powiśle district near the Vistula River and historic parks, the 150 square meter (1,615 square foot) apartment was designed for a young family and includes a primary suite with a walk-in closet and bathroom, as well as a second bedroom, guest bathroom, powder room, pantry, and living area. Here, natural materials, custom furnishings, and a considered collection of art and design pieces shape a home that feels at once personal and connected to the surrounding greenery just outside. 

Inside, the living area opens toward the adjacent park, thanks to large windows that frame the nearby trees while also bringing in natural light to the space. Sheer curtains also provide privacy while allowing soft daylight to filter through, further connecting the interior to its natural setting. Throughout the apartment, a muted palette of taupe, off-white, and dark brown creates an understated backdrop for the family’s collection of furniture and art. Brown-stained oak, stone, and sand-textured wall finishes introduce subtle variations in texture, while the natural grain of wood and the expressive veining of marble bring depth to an otherwise restrained palette.

Many of the apartment’s furnishings were custom-designed by Oskar Firek Architects, including an entrance console with integrated seating, a steel Brutalist sideboard, coffee and dining tables, and a bedroom desk. These bespoke elements sit alongside a selection of contemporary and vintage design, including a Henge pendant above the dining table, Gubi chairs, an Audo Copenhagen armchair, and a 1970s Slovak Brutalist armchair. Art also introduces another layer to the interiors, reflecting the studio’s longstanding connection to creative practice: sculptures, paintings, and ceramic objects appear throughout the residence, including works by Paweł Jach, Tomek Opaliński, Wojciech Firek, Grzegorz Worpus, and Marina Arias. 

With the SAR Apartment, Oskar Firek Architects brings together its interests in art, natural materials, refined forms, and functional planning to create a highly individualized interior where architecture, furniture, and art are considered as parts of a cohesive whole.

articles.title: Remembering Jim Waterman, a Boulder web pioneer, water resources engineer and lover of the natural world
articles.summary: James “Jim” Reed Waterman, 69, of Boulder County, Colorado, died on May 13, 2025, after two years in home hospice care. Few knew Jim Waterman well, but if you did, it was profound. He was intelligent, informed, intentional, and extraordinar…
articles.content:
James “Jim” Reed Waterman, 69, of Boulder County, Colorado, died on May 13, 2025, after two years in home hospice care. Few knew Jim Waterman well, but if you did, it was profound. He was intelligent, informed, intentional, and extraordinarily conscientious about the natural world and, like all of us, more complex than this brief tribute will convey.

He was born on July 11, 1955, to Emily Louise (née Morrison) and Guy Van Vorst Waterman in the District of Columbia. The youngest of three boys, Jim’s family spent time hiking, camping and enjoying the beauty of the East Coast. He was a steady but not yet serious student and graduated in 1973 from Marlboro High School, Marlboro, New York.

Jim was introduced to rock climbing very early in life. The Shawangunk Ridge, aka “The Gunks,” was his climbing center, and he was inspired by a group of naked, climbing daredevils known as the “Vulgarians.” His young mind was also entranced by J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, which he would quote at every opportunity. Long before the movies were made, Jim imagined the landscape and drew recreations of Tolkien’s maps of Middle-earth. Also as a teenager, he crisscrossed the country powered by his thumb with his possessions on his back. His passion for rock climbing led him to the Rocky Mountains and Boulder. It was true love, and, following high school, Boulder County became Jim’s forever home.

During a hectic Boulder roommate search in 1976, applicants were met by a group of Jim’s astrologer friends who calculated birth charts to determine the contender’s compatibility with Jim and another roommate. The charismatic Kathleen Cassaday was chosen. It was the auspicious start of a 49-year relationship filled with love and admiration, adventure, and countless hours together in the garden. Kathleen and Jim married in 1985, and she was by his side when he took his last breath.

Jim first worked both in kitchens and construction, but soon realized life as an engineer would be more sustainable, and he made the call to enroll at the University of Colorado Boulder. He was a powerhouse student but truly, it came so easily to him. He graduated with a civil engineering degree in 1985 and became a member of Chi Epsilon, the Civil Engineering Honor Society. Jim was then awarded a Chancellor’s Fellowship, allowing him to add a master’s degree to his resume. Throughout his career he worked for the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), the Center for Advanced Decision Support for Water and Environmental Systems (CADSWES), the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), and the City of Boulder and Boulder County. In 1992, the BLM presented him with The Citizen Award for his contributions.

Jim was also a pioneer of the World Wide Web. The Boulder Community Network (BCN) launched in March 1994 as only the world’s second web-based community network that brought together local institutions and volunteers to put Boulder-area information and applications online just as the Web was emerging. Jim joined the effort immediately. He became one of BCN’s core technical leaders, serving on its board, coordinating its Technical Committee, and developing its environmental and weather resources.

He later led the technical development of BASIN, the Boulder Area Sustainability Information Network, which brought together water-quality, streamflow, watershed research, maps, and other environmental data from the City of Boulder, the U.S. Geological Survey, and other local partners for public use on the Web. The EPA later used BASIN as a national case study in its 2001 handbook Delivering Timely Environmental Information to Your Community. He also created DIPP (Distributed Information Processing Protocol), an early system that allowed BCN’s community volunteers to maintain Web content themselves without having to become Unix system administrators. He remained one of BCN’s mainstays for decades. Jim was immensely proud of both his contributions to BCN and to water resource engineering.

Jim also found peace and contentment in nature. Whether alone or with Kathleen in tow, he traveled in his beloved, trusty Tacoma to access hiking and camping in the backcountry. He was in awe of arches and spent vacations exploring the Colorado Plateau. On desert hikes, Jim would often take long breaks, sit in the shade — freshly rolled cigarette in hand — and take in the beauty of his surroundings.

Back at home, Jim and Kathleen nurtured a bountiful, organic garden. Jim cultivated the soil while Kathleen tended to the plants, and their hard work paid dividends in raspberries, corn, tomatoes, and cucumbers – all of Jim’s favorite fruits and vegetables. Pickling and canning extended the harvest through many months each year.

This story would not be complete without mentioning Jim’s ability to excel at Jeopardy!, a dinnertime ritual for him and Kathleen. Not surprising really, because he was knowledgeable on so many topics and had a laser-sharp memory. Jim had a “great life of the mind,” and it made for lively and engaging conversations.

He was a man of many talents, known for his ability to tackle projects with precision. His analytical mind anticipated challenges, allowing him to visualize solutions to problems before they arose. Jim could critically dissect the movies he watched and books he read and was a voracious consumer of current affairs which also came under his scrutiny. He kept up with the condition of the Western watersheds, which added to his skepticism that “things were going well” with our planet.

Among the deepest sorrows of Jim’s life was the tragic loss of his older brothers, William “Bill” Antonio Waterman in 1973 and John Mallon Waterman in 1981, both of whom tragically disappeared in the Alaskan wilderness.

Jim was extremely compassionate and could be generous in unusual ways. He was a longtime monthly contributor to KGNU Community Radio – a station to which he faithfully listened. Kathleen asks that you honor Jim’s legacy with a gift to the station in his name.

Jim will make his final journey eastward and be interred along with his mother in the Reed family plot at Woodlawn Cemetery, Canandaigua, New York.

“Let children walk with nature, let them see the beautiful blending and communion of death and life; their joyous inseparable unity, as taught in woods and meadows, plains and mountains and streams of our blessed star, and learn that death is stingless indeed and as beautiful as life.”

—John Muir
Talkeetna Climbers’ Memorial, Alaska

The post Remembering Jim Waterman, a Boulder web pioneer, water resources engineer and lover of the natural world appeared first on The Boulder Reporting Lab.

articles.title: Buddhist Organizations Respond to Nepal’s Flash Floods
articles.summary: In the days following the devastating climate emergency in Nepal and Tibet, Buddhist groups in the region and around the world are mobilizing to help those in need. The post Buddhist Organizations Respond to Nepal’s Flash Floods appeared fi…
articles.content:
On the morning of Wednesday, August 26, a flash flood was triggered by a glacier collapsing in Nepal’s Langtang National Park, according to the US Geological Survey. The park is about seventy-five miles north of Kathmandu, and the flood and debris traveled more than fifty miles, sweeping away everything in its path. 

A week later, the death toll in Nepal has reached 1,222 people, and nearly 5,000 people remain missing. On the Tibetan side, the death toll is 21, with more than 540 people unaccounted for, Chinese state media reports.

The Kathmandu Valley is the spiritual home and an important pilgrimage site for Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, Sikhism, Tibetan Bon, and other religions and traditions. Pilgrims, including those on their way to Mount Kailash, are among the missing. In Kathmandu, people are pinning photos and descriptions of missing loved ones, while mass burials are held, sometimes with straw effigies in place of the missing.  

Earlier this week, Tricycle briefly corresponded with Rockey Tripathi, a volunteer in Nepal associated with Bodhi Institute and many other institutions in Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha.  

“Yes, we are doing the first response, but it’s just very difficult to access the flooded area due to road blockages and also constant threat of landslides,” wrote Tripathi, who went to Galchi, Dhading District, to help with aid distribution following the floods. Tripathi and the other volunteers from Lumbini also responded to the 2015 Nepal earthquake and the Covid-19 pandemic.

“We are preparing to go and rebuild, clean and tidy the houses for flood victims (for) as many requests that need helping hands,” Tripathi said, adding he plans to help with additional support and supplies for those living in government temporary housing, especially for children, women, and girls. (Tripathi is the brother of Venerable Metteyya Sakyaputta, a monk in Lumbini whose work supports local women through training programs and young nuns through Peace Grove Nunnery.) 

When asked how best to support the relief effort, Tripathi suggested donating through Anatta World Health, a US nonprofit, or the Canadian Engaged Buddhist Organization. 

Friends of Tricycle have also recommended donating to the following organizations:

  • Government of Nepal Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund 
  • Buddhist Global Relief (the organization has made crisis relief donations to Karuna Shechen and World Central Kitchen) 
  • Rokpa International (link to donating in US dollars)  
  • Tzu Chi USA 
  • Foundation for the Preservation of Mahayana Teachings’ Emergency Relief Fund
  • Lumbini Social Services

Adhikaar, a women-led community and workers organization that serves the Nepali-speaking community of New York, has compiled a list of emotional support resources, including the contact information of chaplains and community organizations, and has hosted community gatherings at their Woodside, Queens, center. Adhikaar has also shared a link to a database of missing and located people, including foreign nationals.

UPDATE, 9/8/2026: On Thursday, September 3, a 4.7-magnitude earthquake was detected in Tibet, according to the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam, Germany. Spokesperson Heinrich Hecht told Tricycle that, contrary to other reporting, the earthquake was measured 700 km northeast of the flood area. 

The post Buddhist Organizations Respond to Nepal’s Flash Floods appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.

articles.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?
articles.summary: Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matc…
articles.content:
Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app users to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

Perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user says they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

articles.title: Subjective Perspective Makes Objective Reality ‘Everywhere Whole’
articles.summary: The post Subjective Perspective Makes Objective Reality ‘Everywhere Whole’ appeared first on NOEMA.
articles.content:
Earlier this month, the Berggruen Institute gathered religious scholars, philosophers, quantum physicists, AI technologists, neuroscientists and science fiction novelists at Casa dei Tre Oci in Venice to ponder the nature of consciousness. It is fascinating to see how their ideas correspond to the long-ago musings of Medieval mystics and even the “pagan masters” of antiquity.

These reflections across time mirror each other. The great question then, as now, and probably forever, is whether there is a metaphysical gap between the body and the soul, or if they are made of the same substance, symbiotic aspects of a singular reality that entail each other.

Religious Awareness: One Reality, Many Forms

Religious thinkers tend to see consciousness, or “the birth of God in the soul,” as a recognition of the eternal, encompassing fabric of the universe that infuses all Being, even as the physical forms and functions that manifest it are endlessly differentiated.

This is apparent already in the obscure classic, “Book of 24 Philosophers,” published in the 12th century, with some contributions said to have originated in the 3rd and 4th centuries. According to Peter Sloterdijk, in that tome of arresting aphorisms authored by unnamed pagan thinkers, “God is an infinite sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.” As the German philosopher observes, this formless conception befuddles the human spatial imagination because “God is neither contained in anything that contains him, nor is there anything outside him … he has no beyond, no outside. If the center is everywhere, it is everywhere whole.”

In another passage cited by Sloterdijk, God is the singular presence that courses through existence as omnipresent in all phenomena: “God is the monad that begets a monad and bends back upon itself in a single glowing breath.”

In Venice, the religious scholars and a Chinese thinker echoed this cosmology.

Swami Medhananda, a monk of the Ramakrishna Order, concisely frames even older Indian spirituality in this context.

“Hinduism has no single creed. Yet I suggest that four broad ideas, deeply rooted in Hindu scriptures and cutting across sectarian boundaries, express its universal spiritual core:

  1. The Divine is one infinite Reality, both personal and impersonal, known by many names and approached in many forms.
  2. Our deepest identity is spiritual — the immortal ātman, intimately connected with the Divine — and we suffer because we mistake the changing body, mind and ego for our true self.
  3. Life’s highest goal is mokṣa — freedom from ignorance, suffering and rebirth — through direct realization of the Divine and our relationship with it.
  4. The infinite Divine can be realized through infinitely many paths.”

He elaborated: “A celebrated verse from the ‘Rig Veda’ says, ekam sad viprā bahudhā vadanti: ‘Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.’ To capture this non-sectarian vision, I have coined the term polymorphic monism: Hinduism affirms one infinite Divine Reality that can be known and worshipped in many forms.

“’Monism’ is important. Monotheism affirms one supreme personal God, whereas Hindu monism is broader, encompassing both personal and impersonal aspects of the Divine. It includes saguṇa Brahman — the Divine with qualities — worshipped in forms such as Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Ganesha and Christ; the formless personal Divine affirmed in Islam, Sikhism and some Hindu traditions; and nirguṇa Brahman, the impersonal, attributeless, nondual Reality beyond every name and form.”

Presence & Existence

In his intervention, Muhammed U. Faruque draws on Sufism and Islamic philosophy to argue that subjective experience presupposes a deeper, non-objectifiable ground called “presence” (ḥuḍūr).

“In the absence of external stimuli,” he says, “consciousness itself becomes the only ‘light,’ revealing your presence. Consciousness is self-illuminating and self-cognizing, i.e., it knows itself directly, without any intermediary or subject-object division. Just as light makes other things visible, consciousness discloses both the self and the world, but unlike light, it is also aware of itself. Consequently, the essence of consciousness lies not primarily in qualia, but in its intrinsic presence and capacity for self-knowledge, which constitute the fundamental reality of the self and provide the basis for all other forms of cognition. 

 “Within human experience, the consciousness of the ‘I’ is unique, simple, and indivisible. Although we may experience a variety of thoughts and emotions, even seemingly conflicting emotions such as happiness and sadness at the same time, the subject who experiences them remains one and the same. Also, it is impossible to add another consciousness of ‘I’ to one’s own awareness or to divide the ‘I’ into multiple conscious entities. This unity points to the simplicity of self-awareness, that is, the self is not a composite of separate centers of consciousness but a single, irreducible subject of experience. 

 “Human subjectivity is both empty and total. It is ‘empty’ because the contents of consciousness such as thoughts, feelings, memories, and perceptions are not identical with the conscious subject and can therefore change without altering the underlying ‘I.’ Yet it is also ‘total’ because every object of experience appears only within consciousness. In this sense, the entire universe is disclosed through the knowing subject.

“There is no reason to think that consciousness comes into existence only when there is an I-consciousness in relation to an external object, since our logical sense demands that consciousness must exist first, in order that it may become self-conscious by the knowledge of objects with which it contrasts itself. Consciousness can only be the underlying subject in all of our experiences; hence, it must be more fundamental than both our reflective and intersubjective (involving multiple) experiences. In my theory, consciousness is a multimodal phenomenon having nonreflective, reflective, and intersubjective modes.”

Song Bing, the Berggruen Institute’s president who formerly led the Institute’s China Center at Peking University, makes a similar case, substituting Faruque’s “presence” with the notion of “Existence.”

“All scientific observations and analyses are shaped by perception, and are subjective in nature.

“Perception keeps changing; however, the functioning of perceiving appears constant in each occurrence. Therefore, the capacity giving rise to such functioning must remain unchanged. It follows that the perceiver or “I”, which possesses such capacity, must also be unchanged. It is ever-present and remains unchanged. It is what Liu Fenghe — the contemporary wisdom teacher — has termed Existence. 

“Existence is without arising or ceasing. It inherently possesses all capacity and gives rise to all functioning. All arising, changing, and ceasing are the functioning of Existence and are dependent upon Existence. While all perceptions change constantly, Existence remains unchanged.”

Consciousness As An ‘Internal Film,’ ‘Controlled Hallucination’ Or ‘Confabulation’

Philosopher Jenann Ismael attempts to square the circle of the big question with the metaphor of a mirror.

“Is consciousness the ground of everything,” she asks, “with the material world just a pattern woven out of regularities in experience? Or is matter the ground of everything, with consciousness a kind of internal film produced by the machinery of the brain? I suspect the answer is both — that consciousness and matter are not rival foundations but the subjective and objective faces of a single existence.

“Picture a mirror on the far wall of a room. There is the room itself, ordinary and three-dimensional, and there is the mirror, a flat surface mounted on the wall, in which the room appears. The mirror’s surface belongs to both realities at once. It is a kind of membrane between them, separating the room reflected in the mirror from the room that does the reflecting. That, I want to suggest, is the peculiar status of our experience: it is the membrane between an inner and an outer world, at once containing the whole of reality within it and occupying, by its own account, only a thin sliver of that reality.”

With Ismael’s notion of self-awareness as an “internal film” produced by our sensory apparatus in mind, neuroscientist Anil Seth offers where he has landed on the big question after a quarter of a century studying consciousness.

“My own work on consciousness, which goes back about 25 years, follows one single and powerful idea,” Seth argues. “This is the idea that the brain is a prediction machine, and every conscious experience we have — whether of the world, or of the self — is a kind of controlled hallucination: a brain-based best-guess that is tied to reality by signals coming into the brain from the senses. In this view, what we experience comes as much from the ‘inside out’ and from the ‘outside in’, and we don’t experience the world as it really is, but in ways that help us to survive and thrive. As the novelist Anaïs Nin once said: ‘We don’t see things as they are, we see them as we are.’

“With a deeper understanding of consciousness comes the chance to reconcile with the impermanence of the ever-changing bundle of perceptual experiences that we call ourselves and that define our worlds. The line ‘I open my eyes and a world appears’ comes from my book ‘Being You.’ The poet Sylvia Plath closes the circle: ‘I shut my eyes and all of the world drops dead.’”

The idea of consciousness as an “internal film” or “controlled hallucination” fits snugly with science fiction novelist Ken Liu’s view of consciousness as the ability to confabulate. 

“Since consciousness is a subjectively experienced state, no one can judge whether it is ‘real’ except the agent experiencing it,” Liu says.

“We may be able to bypass the quintessentially subjective nature of consciousness by some expedient and reduce it to functional tests, behavioral proxies, neural signatures, etc. — in a word, define the subjectivity away. But I don’t think what we would then be defining is consciousness, only a shadow. The ‘I’ that drives everything remains behind the gaze, impossible to pin down.”

Here, Liu muses, the attempt to construct thinking machines is useful. “Constructing thinking machines will help us better understand our own neural circuitry. For instance, one feature of conscious experience involves storytelling, or confabulation. This goes all the way down to the way our brain creates a sense of integrated sensory simultaneity despite differences in the time it takes neural signals from different parts of the body to reach the brain, and all the way up to the way we construct our sense of self with a purpose, a history, a yearning for meaning. Our memory requires active reconstruction with each recall. Is this compression-confabulation required for a finite being to experience or articulate infinity? As we try to build thinking machines, we may gain insight into whether the ability to confabulate is essential to a conscious being.”

We Are Fundamental To The Reality We Observe

The quantum physicist Carlo Rovelli argues that the much-discussed metaphysical gap between body and soul, subjective and objective, doesn’t exist. 

As he has written in Noema, “We, subjects of knowledge and understanding, are not outside the world. We are part of it. Our theories and knowledge are embodied tools to help us navigate the real world, not disembodied views on reality from the outside. They are themselves aspects of the very world they describe. Our understanding, like our feelings, perceptions and experience, is a natural phenomenon.”

For Rovelli, the notion of a metaphysical gap “contradicts everything we have learned about nature in the last centuries. The mind is the behavior of the brain, properly described in a high-level language. Neither my own experience of myself nor an external experience of me is primary: They are two distinct perspectives on the same events. We do not need to assume that the circle between epistemology (how we get knowledge) and ontology (what exists) requires a starting point. There is nothing wrong with its circularity: The world I access is the information I have about it, and I am part of that world.

“Nor do we need to require that there is any ultimate or fundamental account of reality. Any account is approximate, has blind spots and is realized within reality, so it is embodied in a part of that same reality. 

“If we do not fall into the error of dualism upfront, we can safely speak of soul and emotions just as we speak of a kitchen table, even if the table is also a collection of atoms. It is time to give up the pernicious dualism introduced by the debate on consciousness and embrace the reality that our soul, or our spiritual life, is consistent with our fundamental physics. 

“Earth is not metaphysically different from the heavens, living beings are not metaphysically different from inanimate matter, humans are not metaphysically different from other animals. The soul is not metaphysically different from the body. We are all parts of nature.” 

Rovelli’s scientific case that we humans are not outside the world of reality, but constitutive participants in it and constructors of it, tracks with the intuition of Medieval thinkers like the 14th-century Christian mystic Meister Eckhart. 

For Eckhart, consciousness was being aware we are not apart from, but both inhabit and are inhabited by, the mind of God — that is, “objective reality.” 

As stated in the New Testament’s Gospel of John, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” In biblical terms, the Word, or Logos, is divine reason. Eckhart interpreted this passage as meaning that the incarnation of the divine in man was not a one-time event of Christ’s birth in Bethlehem, but takes place through continuous human participation in the unfolding Logos of the Word, making us part of and conjoining with the mind of God; co-essences, so to speak.” If God is the pure thought of divine reason, then, as Sloterdijk has put it, ‘To think is to give birth to God.’”

That Medieval insight is another way of saying, in Rovelli’s words, that “objectivity without a subject is an abstract construct, of little relevance — it is the illusion of a science now belonging to the past.”

Consciousness, then, can be said to be the perspective of the aware self in a world where there is no outside. The “I” is not detached from some order of objective reality, but in all the diversity of personal experience, part of what makes it “everywhere whole.” Not only is “the universe disclosed by a knowing subject;” the knowing subject is its co-creator from within.

Correction: On Aug. 28, 2026, this essay was changed to reference the Gospel of John rather than Genesis.

articles.title: How Dance Becomes an Offering
articles.summary: Karen Greenspan explores the rich traditions of sacred dance in Vajrayana Buddhism, where movement becomes a way to welcome, invoke, offer, and bless. The post How Dance Becomes an Offering appeared first on Lion’s Roar.
articles.content:
The dancers weave a graceful grapevine step, holding objects of enjoyment mounted on colorful ceremonial scarves — musical instruments, flowers, perfume. Wearing long, silk, Tibetan gowns in bright hues, we circle the ritual mandala in Tara Mandala’s prayer hall in a dance of offering. This sacred dance is part of an elaborate form of inner offering called “Chötreng,” or Garland of Offerings, performed during the “White Dakini Drupchen” a communal ritual of accomplishment.  This evocation of generosity is sung by the chant master and congregation while everyone performs mudras (hand choreography) as they visualize offering and receiving sixteen splendid gifts. These are imagined to be multiplied and delivered by beautiful Wisdom Goddesses, and as such, we dance them.

“The offering of dance to enhance the energy around an occasion is a frequent part of Buddhist life in the Himalayas.”

“Everyone ─ gods and humans alike ─ love dance — just as they love flowers. No one can resist the beauty,” a Bhutanese cham master once told me as he explained why cham (sacred dance) is offered in so many rituals in Vajrayana Buddhism. He was describing the invocatory power of dance ─ the power to call divine qualities into presence. The offering of dance and offerings in general are made to cultivate generosity ─ one of six transcendent qualities, or paramitas. As the Nyingma master Thinley Norbu Rinpoche (1931 –2011) wrote in the liner notes to a cham instruction video he produced, “In the precious Vajrayana tradition, in which the offering of dance is practiced, everything is turned into virtue, including all movement.” 

With the Vajrayana approach, we turn everything, including dance, into a magnificent offering and multiply it with the help of visualization. The offering of dance to enhance the energy around an occasion is a frequent part of Buddhist life in the Himalayas. It’s common to offer a ritual dance to welcome a lama, to invoke a deity’s presence during a ritual, or to boost the auspiciousness of an event. There are numerous examples of this all throughout the region. 

Welcoming the Sacred

In Bhutan, lamas, kings, and VIPs are welcomed to celebrations, prayer events, and public teachings with an escort dance called “Jipai Pawo Cham” (Majestic Hero’s Dance). The dance is performed by two or four pawo (heroes) accompanying the honored guest in procession flanking him or her with joyful sound and movement ─ hopping and bounding with arms raised as they rattle their damaru drums. Upon arriving at the place of ceremonial reception, the dancers stand before the honored guest and perform the complete dance, including peaceful, semi-wrathful, and wrathful sections, as the serkyem, or ritual libation, is proffered.

Guru Padmasambhava, the Indian tantric master also known as Guru Rinpoche who brought Buddhism to Tibet and Bhutan in the mid-8th century, is invoked during many prayer gatherings and Tsechu (Guru Rinpoche Day) celebrations with a cham called “Zheng Zhik Pema.” The dancers are costumed as dakas and dakinis, beings who populate Guru Rinpoche’s Glorious Copper-Colored Mountain Paradise. In this dance-prayer, the dancers spin and jump, sounding their damarus to a declaimed liturgy that the Guru is said to have given to his foremost disciple, Yeshe Tsogyal, as a means of summoning him instantly.

During the daylong Tsechu Puja that honors Guru Padmasambhava with a full day’s program of sacred cham, the Guru is welcomed and then bid farewell with “Kadrinchenma Cham,” a dance expressing immense gratitude and the longing to see the Guru again and again. The dance-prayer, performed by dakinis, is part of the Tsechu Puja text, a treasure revealed by the great treasure revealer Chokyi Wangchuk (b.1212 – d.1270), and is performed at many Nyingma and Kagyu monasteries. 

Dance to Increase Auspiciousness

Under the leadership of His Holiness the Twelfth Gyalwang Drukpa, the Drukpa Kagyu nuns and monks often pack their religious rituals with cham dances to augment the auspiciousness of the events. The Avalokiteshvara Drupchen, a nine-day ritual event dedicated to accomplishing the compassion of Avalokiteshvara, held at Druk Amitabha Mountain in Kathmandu, Nepal, is a case in point. The drupchen ritual, as performed by the Drukpa nuns, is suffused with highly dramatic and peaceful cham dances that were later added to the original ritual text by His Holiness and his father, the Nyingma master Zichen Bairo Rinpoche. This was done to enhance the auspiciousness of the ritual event. And the dances do exactly that. They raise energy by virtue of the preparation and anticipation around them, and afterwards, by the inclination to reflect upon them.

These same nuns and monks perform another genre of dance offering: gurma, or songs of realization. These verses celebrating spiritual life are sung while performing delightful, folksy choreographies. They are frequently presented during special occasions such as grand pujas, formal teachings, completion of long-term retreats, consecration of temples and stupas, and birth and death anniversaries of lineage masters. The Drukpa nuns include these as a regular offering during their feast day pujas twice a month. 

Sacred dance is also offered as an homage and welcome to monks and nuns when they come out of long-term retreat. The Drukpa Kagyu monks and nuns mentioned above perform a set of gurma dances to celebrate the return of retreatants. On this occasion, they dance wearing the repa sash — a white, cotton wrap — of accomplished tantric yoga practitioners draped over their monastic robes. In a similar gesture, the Karma Kagyu nuns of Karma Drubdey Nunnery in Trongsa, Bhutan, welcome their returning yoginis by performing “Khandro Denga Cham” (Cham of the Five Dakinis) as well as a gurma dance to a composition by the 11th century yogi and poet Milarepa. 

In Himalayan Buddhism, prayers requesting that a spiritual teacher remain in this world are frequently composed and recited because the teacher’s longevity is considered the practitioners’ best opportunity for enlightenment. “Khandro Denga Cham,” also called “Khandro Tenzhug” (Long life Prayer to the Dakinis), is a component of longevity rituals meant to remove obstacles to the long life of great lamas, spiritual teachers, and all beings. The tradition holds that the dakinis and other celestial beings, meanwhile, desire these great teachers to move on to other buddha realms and summon them to leave this life. “Khandro Tenzhug” is performed as an offering to the dakinis to allay their call and prolong the life of the lama.

The Vedic Roots of Ritual Dance

Vedic wisdom and practice provided the foundations for many of the ritual conventions that were absorbed into early Buddhism and are still practiced today. The Vedas, a body of early sacred and philosophical Hindu texts composed during the period of about 1500–1200 BCE, attest to a pre-Buddhist cultural context in which music and dance were woven into the fabric of ritual practice, spiritual contemplation, and cosmic understanding. The Yajur Veda, a compilation of rituals, offering formulas, and mantras, contains references to the rhythmic recitation of mantras during rituals. Fast forward to Vajrayana deity yoga, systematized by Indian commentators circa 700 CE, where one still chants a recitation in Sanskrit (even in Tibetan texts) of making offerings while performing representative mudras, or hand gestures. This embodied activity is part of the visualization technique used to invite the deity into presence. Frequently the texts elaborate the visualization with celestial offering goddesses, who multiply and enhance the offering activity.

In the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal, where the Vajrayana Buddhism of the Newar (indigenous inhabitants of the valley) people has a distinctive South Asian flavor, these offering goddesses bestow their bliss offerings through a dance. The Newar Buddhist priestly caste of vajracharyas (non-monastic priests) have, for at least a thousand years, practiced a yogic dance tradition and ritual art called charya nritya, or “dance as a spiritual discipline.” Within this tradition, one performs “Sodasha Lasya” (sixteen expressions of grace) dancing as sixteen offering goddesses. The performer dance/mimes offering each item: strumming a lute, playing the flute, beating a drum, placing a mala garland around the deity’s neck, singing a song that vibrates outward from one’s lips, sending plumes of scent from an incense bundle wafting through the air, and more. 

These same offering goddesses make a danced appearance in the Tibetan and Bhutanese traditions in a variety of dances called “Rigma Chudruk Cham” (Dance of the Sixteen Wisdom Goddesses). And the cham I performed called “Chötreng” falls into this category. Each lineage or locale has its own iteration of the cham, performed in beautiful dakini attire ─ a silk brocade robe with a set of bone ornaments, including an apron, armlets, wristlets, necklaces, a chest emblem, and crown. For centuries, the dance was performed by monks dressed as these female wisdom beings because monks populated the religious institutions where these dances were performed. It is only over the last twenty years that female practitioners have been invited to perform this and other dakini cham ─ both within nunneries in the Himalayas and at a handful of dharma centers in the East and West. 

Dancing to Bestow Good Wishes

Finally, I return to the Drukpa Kagyu nuns and monks, who frequently conclude large ceremonial events with a gurma called “Tashi Cham” to dispense wishes of auspiciousness. Whereas it is customary for prayer services to conclude with a prayer extending tashi (auspiciousness) to all beings, the Drukpa monastics dance it with gusto. Holding in each hand a set of streamers in the five colors representing the five natural elements and five wisdoms, they move in a circle tossing their arms and streamers in spirals like giant paint brushes. With their stomping feet, they crush negativity and with their arms, they stir up joy while singing lyrics that describe the Five Wisdom Buddhas arriving from their five directions bringing good fortune to all sentient beings. Each verse resounds with the refrain, “How delightful and joyful!” This heartfelt tashi is delivered with body, speech, and mind  ─ the three doors that all sacred dance integrates. Just as generosity is a transcendent virtue, so too are the dances that deliver its boundless goodness.

articles.title: DD399 / Not a machine: on fragility and self-worth
articles.summary: Issue 399: Not a machine: on fragility and self-worth – Read the full issue in the archive.
articles.content:
My mum recently had orthopaedic surgery, and although the German infrastructure is about as good as it gets, she’s now getting a crash course in what it’s like to move through the world as a disabled person – hopefully just for a while.

For someone with a lifelong, stubborn belief that she’s fine without help from others, it’s taken some adjusting. It brought to mind this quote: ‘The disability community is the only minority group that anyone can join at any time.’

Aptly timed, this essay by disabled writer and artist vōx landed at the top of my reading list. It’s about the grief of no longer being economically useful, and how tightly we’ve bound a person’s worth to their output.

vōx traces this back all the way to the Protestant work ethic, the idea that hard work and discipline are signs of virtue. The theology is mostly gone, but the residue is everywhere, repackaged as hustle podcasts and 5am routines:

“The ideal person under capitalism is tireless, independent, resilient, endlessly capable of overriding their own limits in service of output. You may be severely injured and anemic but don’t you dare skip gym day.”

“When you become chronically ill or disabled, you begin to understand how deeply this ideology has embedded itself into the psyche. The shame of no longer being able to work consistently feels personal. As though my body’s inability to keep pace with capitalism says something fundamental about who I am.”

“It’s there every time you meet someone new and one of their first questions is, ‘What do you do?’ They’re not asking about your passions, your hobbies, or the mundane human tasks that take up most of your time. They’re asking how you make money. How you turn yourself into income.”

“In this way, illness strips people not only of income but of social legitimacy. I didn’t just lose the ability to work consistently. I lost the cultural permission to feel worthy.”

vōx’s writing catalogues what gets lost when a body can’t keep pace with what capitalism expects of it – income, obviously, but also the plain social permission to feel worthwhile.

I keep thinking about my mum learning to ask strangers for help, decades of ‘rugged individualism’ undone in a week. It’s not just help she’s resisting, but what needing it seems to say about her worth.

She will likely walk again soon. Given her age though, this is less an injury than a preview. None of us get to opt out of this forever – no matter how ambitious or disciplined we are. The sooner we work out who we are without the output, the softer the transition.

And now to this week’s discoveries. – Kai

articles.title: Case Study: Innovations to green smart cities from Copenhagen to Lima
articles.summary: In 1996, the late architect and theorist Christopher Alexander – muse to the revered producer Brian Eno – addressed a conference room of computer programmers and proposed a future “in which computers play a fundamental role in making the wo…
articles.content:
In 1996, the late architect and theorist Christopher Alexander – muse to the revered producer Brian Eno – addressed a conference room of computer programmers and proposed a future “in which computers play a fundamental role in making the world – and above all the built structure of the world – alive, humane, ecologically profound, and with a deep living structure.”

Deeply inspired by nature, Christopher spent much of his practice thinking about how to evoke belonging and wellbeing – senses he felt were critical to human happiness – in his work.1 To him, there was no contradiction with technology; in fact, he saw programming as the “natural genetic infrastructure of a living world,” and programmers as having critical knowledge and skills to help make better buildings, cities and spaces available for everyone.

A decade later, tech giants IBM and Cisco proposed the concept of ‘smart cities’ to address urban issues. In their vision of the smart city, sensors, analytics and computational networks would be used to make cities – the hubs of the future – more efficient and effective. But while living in cities may be the more environmentally efficient way to house millions of people, as Christopher pointed out in his speech, computational technology is simply a tool. So how could embedding technology in cities help us manage the climate crisis, rather than simply encoding existing inequalities, or distracting from structural problems? How could it be used to create the “alive, humane, ecologically profound” world he describes?

Taking a systems approach to electricity in Copenhagen, Denmark

Jutting out into the Øresund Strait, just north of Copenhagen’s city centre, lies Nordhavn, where the sun flashes off glassy new mid-rise apartments arranged in precise, geometric arrangements in this sea-bound neighbourhood. Only 15 years ago, this area was a former industrial shipyard, until the publicly owned CPH City & Port Development Corporation decided to rezone it with the ambition of creating a city-within-a-city that was not just optimised for liveability but also sustainability.

As part of this Cinderella-style transformation, the corporation supported EnergyLab Nordhavn, a four-year living experiment that brought together the city government, universities, utility providers and private businesses to prove how electricity, heat and transport could be integrated into a full-scale smart energy system.

The results were positive: the lab’s final report showed how grid-connected batteries could efficiently store electricity sourced from renewables, while shared real-time data could regulate the output of electricity. Additionally, electric vehicles, including buses, could not only benefit from this power storage but also feed back into the system via vehicle-to-grid technology. And by integrating heat pumps, the system was able to more efficiently heat homes and water.

The system worked so well, in fact, it helped turn Nordhavn into Copenhagen’s priciest neighbourhood. Luckily, at least 25% of the neighbourhood has affordable rental housing, and initiatives like the heat pumps are now being rolled out across more homes in Copenhagen.

Cleaning the air for children in Lima, Peru

Air pollution may sometimes be hard to see, but its consequences can no doubt be felt. According to the World Health Organisation, more than one in four deaths of children under the age of five globally are related to pollution. But tackling an intangible, invisible problem is easy to de-prioritise. While cities from Seoul to Santiago have installed air monitors to more accurately track the issue, until recently, the cost of installing and maintaining enough devices to make such a system useful have dissuaded many more cities from using them.

But thanks to lowering costs of air sensors, in 2020, the city of Lima was able to build out its network, and install 35 new devices in a program specifically designed to improve air quality for young children. The city installed sensors in kindergartens, schools, hospitals and paediatric centres, complemented with mobile monitors set at a height of 95 cm to more accurately assess the amount of pollution children are exposed to.

Several schools and children’s shelters in Lima were able to adjust their schedules so that children could play outside when pollution levels were lower. Other solutions were more targeted: after sensors showed particularly high levels of pollution around a school in one of the city’s lower-income neighbourhoods, the city took action and agreed with neighbours to plant green mulch and pave roads to reduce pollution.

Streamlining transport in Berlin, Germany

Enter the idea of Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS). At its heart, MaaS is an all-in-one system, usually accessed through an app, that helps you get from A to B via the best combination of transit options, and allows you to pay for it.2

In Berlin, you could use Google maps – or you could use Jelbi, an app that looks like a mix of Google maps, Uber, and Neuron or Lime. You could then either order a taxi, or head to one of Jelbi’s bright, endorphin-releasing yellow hubs with electric bikes and scooters – some even have electric cars charging waiting to be borrowed – and head on your way, thanks to the world’s most extensive MaaS network. 

So far, Berlin has led the way in successfully implementing MaaS. In 2015, a private startup in Helsinki launched the first MaaS app, Whim, but limited cooperation from the state’s rail service stymied the attractiveness of the service.3 In contrast, in Berlin, it was the city’s public transport company BVG who led the way, pairing with Lithuanian software company Trafi to launch Jelbi. Meanwhile, keeping a car for a weekend getaway out of the city may also soon be redundant – Switzerland’s yumuv, also designed by Trafi, connects regional commuters and travellers between Zurich, Basel and Bern via intercity train.

But having a MaaS system that truly serves the people using it means understanding how people use it, what they need it for, and having the correct infrastructure to support this in the first place. In 2022, while Brussels trialled a prototype of its current app Floya, researchers from the University of Antwerp looked at transport access and equity from the perspective of families, pointing out that nearly 40 percent of the city’s households include children. Conducting a small sample study, they found that their respondents had no trouble with what officials often named as common barriers to using MaaS, like not being app-savvy, or not being comfortable with using multiple modes of transport. Rather, they were more concerned about not being able to board a tram easily if an older, non-accessible model arrived; no elevator access at train stations; or not having shelter at bus stops. With transport currently contributing to 15 percent of greenhouse gases, changing how we get around to shared forms of transport will be essential to addressing climate change.           

Supporting new technologies in New York City, United States

What if there was a device that could suck the pollution out of the air? Or what if a drone could scan a building and use laser technology to see if its structure could be retrofitted to improve energy efficiency?

These technologies do exist, but there’s no better way to know if an idea works than to put it to the test – so that’s what New York City’s Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI) did, as part of their Smart City Testbed program. Trials to monitor anonymous travel paths, scan buildings, and use negative-ion devices to reduce air pollution started in October 2023, and the city piloted them for six to eight months.

Lokesh Jain, the managing director of the Netherlands-based company producing the ionisers, StaticAir, said the Smart City Testbed program was also useful because it addressed one of the biggest challenges of installing new challenges in cities: the bureaucratic process. In this case, OTI coordinated the approvals required from all necessary departments.

At nearly €4000 (AU$6,500) per device, the ionisers are not designed to blanket a city, but rather, target pollution hotspots as part of a coordinated solution – another reason to welcome bureaucratic support. The company has already installed their devices in several cities around the world, including Athens and Rotterdam, but the results of the NYC trial will provide another example of how authorities, their departments and private companies can work together to test out new solutions. After all, it’s one thing to prove a technology works in isolation, but it’s another to use it in real life situations so that people can actually benefit. 


Tools for the future

The United Nations expects that nearly 70 percent of the world’s population will be living in cities by 2050, allowing us to tackle the climate crisis in more efficient ways. But cities and people, unlike computers, are ambiguous and constantly changing. In the years since IBM and Cisco first began developing their idea of the ‘smart city’, one major lesson has been clear: successful smart city initiatives need to focus on the ‘city’ too, and the needs, desires and agency of the people who live there.

By learning from different initiatives around the world, working with authorities, public and private enterprises and communities to adapt these ideas to how locals live, any smart city can be a smart city.  After all, it’s not the technology that makes a city – it’s the people. And, as Christopher Alexander said back in 1996, if society could ensure technology were used to benefit humanity and nature, “that would be remarkable. It would turn the world around, and make living structure the norm once again, throughout society, and make the world worth living in again.”

  1. Both a theorist and a working practitioner, Christopher Alexander outlined his experiences in his many published works, including A City is Not a Tree (1965) and the four-volume series The Nature of Order (2002–2004).
  2. Options include paying either per leg of the journey, or via monthly subscription.
  3. Online, a city planner for the City of Helsinki anonymously admitted that even they didn’t use it.
The post Case Study: Innovations to green smart cities from Copenhagen to Lima first appeared on Assemble Papers.
